extraction_notes.note: The four 'Statistical Conditions' use a custom \begin{stat} environment that latex_facts does not report; extracted as assumption nodes (confidence 0.9) and their \ref uses added by hand.

Wrong refs in the source: 'Assumption~\ref{eq:regime}' points at equation (15) inside the proof of Proposition MLE instead of ass:regime, and 'Lemma~\ref{prob:ws_det}' points at the problem display; the ref edges the finishing step derives from them are kept as stated.

Appendix (sub)sections titled 'Proof of ...' were each extracted as one proof node with their subsections as steps (whole-section rule), so auxiliary lemmas, problems and Algorithm 5 stated there are nested inside proofs; Lemma main_bound is also used outside (Section 12 proofs).

Lemmas main_det, main_feasible, main_lower and Remark rem:lm are stated inside the 'Sketch of the proof' block of Theorem main, so they are nested in that sketch proof node although the full proofs use them.
Remark rem:lm retyped as claim: it asserts a bound on l that Appendix 9.2 proves.

The proof of Theorem network is spread over the opening of Appendix 12 (regular case and plan, WLOG reduction) and the final subsubsection; extracted as three proof parts, with the notation paragraphs between them as Level-1 definitions and problem P_N^L.
Table 1 values, Figures, the numerical discussion of Section 5.1, the real-data study (Section 5.2, Appendix 10) and computational results of Section 6.4 are empirical and were not turned into nodes.
The proof-logic diagram of Theorem network (Figure fig:proof_network) is omitted from the source; dependencies were taken from the lemma statements and proofs instead.

nodes.name: Clinical trials
nodes.statement: Due to the increasing complexity of late-stage randomized clinical trials, the average number of sites required to recruit sufficient subjects for meaningful treatment and control comparisons has grown to over 70-100 per trial \citep{brogger2022changes, basubenchmarking}. At the same time, clinical trials are risky: 80\% of sites fail to meet their recruitment timeline \citep{johnson2015evidence}, and up to 20\% cease due to inadequate recruitment \citep{carlisle2015unsuccessful}.
nodes.statement_short: Clinical-trial site selection: many sites needed, and many fail to recruit, motivating learning which sites succeed.

nodes.name: Retail stores
nodes.statement: Many retail stores close every year due to demographic, economic, and competitive factors. Thus, retailers need to learn the drivers of store performance and adaptively select locations for new stores to maximize coverage, sales and profitability.

nodes.name: Sustainable infrastructure
nodes.statement: Decarbonization pathways require large-scale infrastructure investments across renewable generation, electric vehicle chargers, and industrial equipment \citep{national2021accelerating}. Yet, around 5-10\% of infrastructure projects are canceled or distressed, amounting to significant capital losses \citep{sakhrani2015negotiated}. This again requires adaptive decision-making to learn the characteristics of successful projects and inform future investments.
nodes.statement_short: Infrastructure projects are often cancelled, so investments must learn which projects succeed.

nodes.name: Standard asymptotic notation
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, we adopt standard asymptotic notation: (i) $f(x)=\mathcal{O}(g(x))$ if there exist $M>0$ and $\bar{x}$ such that $f(x)\leq Mg(x)$ for all $x\geq\bar{x}$; (ii) $f(x)=o(g(x))$ if for all $M>0$ there exists $\bar{x}$ such that $f(x)\leq Mg(x)$ for all $x\geq\bar{x}$; (iii) $f(x)=\Omega(g(x))$ if there exist $M>0$ and $\bar{x}$ such that $f(x)\geq Mg(x)$ for all $x\geq\bar{x}$; and (iv) $f(x)=\Theta(g(x))$ if $f(x)=\mathcal{O}(g(x))$ and $f(x)=\Omega(g(x))$.
nodes.section: 3 The online learning and optimization setting
nodes.statement_short: Big-O, little-o, Big-Omega and Big-Theta notation as x grows.

nodes.name: Candidate facilities
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote the set of $M$ candidate facilities.

nodes.name: Coverage target and horizon
nodes.statement: A decision-maker targets to open $m$ facilities over $T\geq 2$ periods, stored in a set $\mathcal{T}=\{1,\cdots,T\}$.

nodes.name: Opening-attempt variables y_it
nodes.statement_short: Binary variable: 1 if the decision-maker attempts to open facility i at time t.

nodes.name: Success indicator S_it
nodes.statement: Let $S_{it}$ denote the binary indicator of the success of facility $i\in\mathcal{F}$ at time $t\in\mathcal{T}$.

nodes.name: Revealed and independent success
nodes.statement: We assume that success is revealed by the next period and is independent across facilities.

nodes.name: Open-facility variables z_it
nodes.statement_short: z_it = 1 iff facility i is attempted at t and succeeds.

nodes.name: Definition of z_it
nodes.statement: z_{it} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if facility $i\in\mathcal{F}$ is open at time $t\in\mathcal{T}$, i.e. if}\ S_{it} = 1 \;\; \text{and}\;\; y_{it}=1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise, i.e., if}\ \text{if}\ S_{it} = 0 \;\; \text{or}\;\; y_{it}=0 \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq:z

nodes.name: Tentative and successful openings A_t, B_t
nodes.statement: Let $A_t=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}y_{it}$ and $B_t=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}z_{it}$ be the number of facilities tentatively and successfully opened at time $t\in\mathcal{T}$, respectively.

nodes.name: Large-target finite-horizon regime
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, we consider the asymptotic regime where $m\to\infty$ but $T\geq2$ is finite.

nodes.name: Asymptotic regime
nodes.statement: As $m \to \infty$, $M=\Omega(m^{3/2})$.
nodes.statement_short: The candidate pool M grows at least like m^{3/2}.
nodes.label: ass:regime

nodes.name: Stationary learning environment
nodes.statement: We consider a stationary learning environment.

nodes.name: Facility success probability eta_i
nodes.statement: We denote by $\eta_{i} \in [0,1]$ the (unknown) probability of success of facility $i\in\mathcal{F}$, so that facility success is governed by a Bernoulli random variable $S_{it}\sim \text{Ber}(\eta_{i})$.

nodes.name: Facility feature vector
nodes.statement: Each facility $i\in\mathcal{F}$ is associated with a feature vector $\boldsymbol{x}_{i} \in \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p_t}$.

nodes.name: Data sample S_t and sample size N_{t-1}
nodes.statement:
The learning population consists of the set of facilities that have been tentatively opened, so the decision-maker has access to the following data sample at each period $t\in\mathcal{T}$, of size $N_{t-1}=\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}A_s$.
$$\mathcal{S}_t=\left\{(\boldsymbol{x}_{i},z_{is})\mid s\in\{1,\cdots,t-1\}\ ;\ i\in\mathcal{F}:y_{is}=1\right\}$$
nodes.statement_short: The online training set at period t: features and outcomes of all facilities tried before t; its size N_{t-1} is the cumulative number of attempts.

nodes.name: Dataset spaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}^n = \mathcal{X}^n\times\{0,1\}^n$ denote the space of datasets of size $n$, and $\mathcal{D} = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{D}^n$ the space of all finite datasets.

nodes.name: Hypothesis set
nodes.statement: We define the set of hypotheses $\mathcal{H} = \{h: \mathcal{X} \to \{0,1\} \mid \Phi(h) \leq 0\}$, where $\Phi(\cdot)$ limits available models.

nodes.name: Classification algorithm
nodes.statement: A classification algorithm $F: \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{H}$ is a function mapping from $ \mathcal{D}$ to $\mathcal{H}$.

nodes.name: Classification model h_t
nodes.statement: The classification model in period $t\in\mathcal{T}$ is denoted by $h_t = F(\mathcal{S}_t)$.

nodes.name: Existence of Positive Samples
nodes.statement: There exists a constant $\xi > 0$ such that at least a fraction $\xi$ of the sample has a success probability greater than $1/2$.
nodes.label: ass:positive

nodes.name: Sampling
nodes.statement: At each time period $t\in\mathcal{T}$, the decision-maker selects facilities randomly with replacement among the set of unexplored facilities with a positive classification, denoted by $\mathcal{J}_t=\{i\in\mathcal{F}\mid y_{i1}=\cdots=y_{i,t-1}=0\ ;\ h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})=1\}$. Thus, $\mathbb{P}\left(y_{it}=1 \mid i \in \mathcal{J}_t\right)= \frac{A_t}{|\mathcal{J}_t|}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each period, facilities are sampled uniformly with replacement from the unexplored, positively classified pool J_t.
nodes.label: ass:sampling

nodes.name: Sampling without replacement
nodes.statement: Alternatively, we could assume that facilities are sampled without replacement, which would induce negative correlation among the $y_{it}$ variables. In that case, standard results from concentration theory \citep{serfling1974probability, bardenet2015concentration} would lead to slightly tighter concentration bounds and all results from the paper would hold.
nodes.statement_short: Sampling without replacement gives negatively correlated selections, tighter concentration, and the same results.

nodes.name: Learning function
nodes.statement: There exists $0<\varepsilon\leq 1$ such that the error of the machine learning model $h_t$ trained with $\mathcal{S}_t$ ($N_{t-1}$ samples) is bounded by: \begin{align*} \mathbb{P}(h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})\neq S_{it} \mid i \in \mathcal{J}_t)=\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} + 1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Misclassification probability of h_t is eps*p/(N_{t-1}+1)^r + eps*(1-p): initial error eps, learning rate r, irreducible share 1-p.
nodes.label: ass:classification

nodes.name: Generative model
nodes.statement: The success probabilities are determined by the features: $\eta_{i} = f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})$, where $f_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]$ is known and $\theta\in\Theta$ is a finite set of parameters.

nodes.name: Margin
nodes.statement: $\mathbb{P}\left(\left|f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\leq\nu\right)\leq C \nu^{\alpha}$ for some $C>0$ and $\alpha>0$.

nodes.name: Regularity
nodes.statement_short: Compact parameter and feature spaces, f twice continuously differentiable in theta, positive definite conditional Fisher information.

nodes.name: Features
nodes.statement:
Features are sampled from distribution $\mathcal{Q}$:
    $\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\sim \mathcal{Q}$.

nodes.name: Bayes-optimal classifier and its error rate
nodes.statement:
We can then define the Bayes-optimal classifier $h^*(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathbf{1}\left\{f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x})>\frac{1}{2}\right\}$ and its error rate $\mu^*$ as follows.  The threshold of $1/2$ arises from symmetric misclassification penalties, but can be easily generalized to any misclassification penalties and any classification threshold.
$$\mu^*=\mathbb{P}(z_{it}\neq1 \mid h^*(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)=1-\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}:\eta_{i}>\frac{1}{2}}f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})}{\left|i\in\mathcal{F}:f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})>\frac{1}{2}\right|}$$
nodes.statement_short: h* thresholds the true success probability at 1/2; mu* is its error rate among positively classified facilities.

nodes.name: Convergence of the online MLE classifier
nodes.statement: Assume that we estimate $\theta$ using the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE): \begin{equation} \widehat{\theta}_t= \argmax_{\theta\in\Theta} \ \prod_{s=1}^{t-1} \prod_{i\in\mathcal{J}_s:y_{is}=1} (f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}))^{z_{is}}(1-f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}))^{1-z_{is}}, \end{equation} and build the classifier $h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}) = \mathbf{1}\left\{f_{\widehat{\theta}_t}(x_{i})>\frac{1}{2}\right\}$. Define the error rate $\mu_t = \mathbb{P}(S_{it}\neq 1 \mid i\in\mathcal{J}_t)$. Assume that $N_t \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ for all $t$. Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:regime}-\ref{ass:sampling} and Statistical Conditions~\ref{ass:known}--\ref{ass:features}, for any $\overline\varepsilon,\gamma>0$, there exists $m_0$ such that for all $m\geq m_0$ and $t\in\mathcal{T}$: \[\mu_t \leq \frac{\overline\varepsilon}{(N_{t-1}+1)^{\min\{\alpha,1\}\times (1/2-\gamma)}}+\mu^*.\]
nodes.statement_short: Under the statistical conditions, the online MLE classifier's error approaches the Bayes error at rate N^{-min(alpha,1)(1/2-gamma)}.
nodes.label: prop:MLE

nodes.name: Maximum likelihood estimator
nodes.statement: \widehat{\theta}_t= \argmax_{\theta\in\Theta} \ \prod_{s=1}^{t-1} \prod_{i\in\mathcal{J}_s:y_{is}=1} (f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}))^{z_{is}}(1-f_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}))^{1-z_{is}},
nodes.label: eq:mle_estimation

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Proposition (MLE convergence)
nodes.statement: The proof (in~\ref{app:stats}) bounds the difference between the classifier's error rate and the Bayes-optimal error by: (i) the sampling probability of each facility across earlier time periods; (ii) the probability that the true success probability lies around 0.5; and (iii) the classifier's error. We show that these terms are respectively bounded by $\mathcal{O}(1/N_{t-1}^{1/2-\gamma})$, $\mathcal{O}(1/N_{t-1}^{\alpha\cdot(1/2-\gamma)})$, or $\mathcal{O}(1/N_{t-1}^{1/2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: decompose the error gap into resampling, margin and estimation terms and bound each.

nodes.name: Proposition matches the learning-function assumption
nodes.statement: Importantly, the upper bound in Proposition \ref{prop:MLE} matches Assumption \ref{ass:classification} with $\varepsilon = \overline\varepsilon + \mu^*$ and $p=\frac{\overline\varepsilon}{\overline\varepsilon+\mu^*}$; the learning rate $\mathcal{O}(1/n^r)$ generalizes the best-case rate of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt n)$ identified in Proposition~\ref{prop:MLE}.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition MLE instantiates the learning function with eps = eps_bar + mu*, p = eps_bar/(eps_bar + mu*).

nodes.name: Learning environment
nodes.statement: Define independent Bernoulli variables $\widetilde{S}_{it}=\mathrm{Bern}\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} + 1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$ and $\widetilde{B}_t = \sum_{i:y_{it}=1} \widetilde{S}_{it}$, with $r=\min\{\alpha,1\} \times \{1/2-\gamma\}$, $\varepsilon = \overline\varepsilon + \mu^*$, and $p = \frac{\overline\varepsilon}{\overline\varepsilon+\mu^*}$. Then, $\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\widetilde{B}_t\geq m\right] \leq \mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^TB_t\geq m\right]$.
nodes.statement_short: Treating the error bound as the actual error rate is conservative for the chance constraint.
nodes.label: cor:learning

nodes.name: Success Distribution
nodes.statement: Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:regime},~\ref{ass:sampling} and \ref{ass:classification}, $B_t$ follows a binomial distribution with $A_t$ trials and success probability $1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} + 1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)$.
nodes.statement_short: B_t is binomial with A_t trials and success probability 1 - eps*p/(N_{t-1}+1)^r - eps*(1-p).
nodes.label: cor:success

nodes.name: Online learning and optimization problem (P*)
nodes.statement:
The problem, referred to as Problem~\eqref{prob:main}, is formulated as:
\begin{align}
    \min_{\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B}}\quad & \sum_{t=1}^T A_t \tag{$\mathcal{P}^*$}\\
    \text{s.t.}\quad&\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^TB_t\geq m\right] \geq 1-\delta \nonumber\\
    \quad& B_t\sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A_t, 1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right),\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber\\
    \quad& A_t,B_t\geq0,\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber
\end{align}
also_stated_at: The decision-maker aims to minimize $\sum_{t=1}^T A_t$ subject to a chance constraint ensuring that $m$ facilities will be opened with high probability: $\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^TB_t\geq m\right]\geq1-\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize total attempted openings subject to a chance constraint that at least m facilities succeed, with learning-dependent binomial successes.

nodes.name: Problem P*

nodes.name: Fully-learned benchmark
nodes.statement: A fully-learned benchmark with error $\varepsilon (1-p)$. In essence, this solves Problem~\ref{prob:main} with parameters $\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(1-p)$ and $p' = 0$.

nodes.name: Fully-learned benchmark opening count
nodes.statement: This benchmark needs to open at least $\frac{m}{1-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)}$ facilities to satisfy the chance constraint.

nodes.name: Regret
nodes.statement: We measure regret against this benchmark.

nodes.name: No-learning baseline
nodes.statement: A no-learning baseline based on a single-stage chance-constrained optimization problem with error $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: No-learning baseline has linear regret
nodes.statement: This benchmark needs to open at least on the order of $\frac{m}{1-\varepsilon}$ facilities, leading to a regret of at least $\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot m$.

nodes.name: Standard normal CDF
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, we denote by $\Phi(\cdot)$ the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution.

nodes.statement: The optimal solution $m^*(\varepsilon, T)$ of Problem~\eqref{prob:main} satisfies, as $m \to \infty$: $$m^*(\varepsilon, T)\geq \begin{cases} c_0\left(m +\max\left\{-\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}, \varepsilon \cdot p \cdot \zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right\}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)\right) & \text{if }p \neq 1,\\ c_0\left(m +\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right) & \text{if }p=1. \end{cases}$$ Algorithm~\ref{ALG} yields an asymptotically feasible solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:main}, achieving an objective of: $$m^\dagger(\varepsilon,T)=\begin{cases} c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \sqrt{\frac{c_0}{2}\log \frac{2}{\delta}}\sqrt{m}\right) & \text{if }p\neq 1,\\ c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right) & \text{if }p=1. \end{cases}$$

nodes.name: Lemma main_lower: lower bound on the optimum
nodes.statement:
Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lower} establishes the lower bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. When $p=1$, the proof shows that $B_t$ remains close to its expected value at each time $t=1,\cdots,T$, using Bernstein's concentration inequality across facilities; it then calls Lemma~\ref{lem:main_det} conditionally on $B_1\approx\mathbb{E}(B_1),\cdots,B_T\approx\mathbb{E}(B_T)$ to bound the total number of facilities $m^*(\varepsilon, T)$. In particular, Bernstein's concentration inequality exploits that the asymptotic error on facility openings is small, so the variance term provides an asymptotically better bound than with Hoeffding's inequality.  When $p\neq1$, it uses the Berry-Esseen theorem to show that the lower bound is necessary to satisfy the chance constraint.

\begin{lemma}[Lower bound] Assume that $\delta = o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)$. Let $m^*(\varepsilon, T)$ denote the optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. The following holds, as $m \to \infty$:
  \[m^*(\varepsilon, T) \geq   \begin{cases}
  c_0\left(m +\max\{-\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m},\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\}\right) & \text{if }p \neq 1\\
      c_0\left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right) & \text{if }p=1
  \end{cases}\]
\end{lemma}

nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:main} provides upper-bounding and lower-bounding approximations of the optimum of Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. nodes.section: 5.1 Discussion of results and managerial implications
nodes.statement_short: Regret is c_0 eps p zeta_T m^{alpha_T(1-r)} to leading order, or Theta(sqrt m) when p<1 and alpha_T(1-r)<1/2.

nodes.name: Long-term regret rate
nodes.statement: With perfect learning ($p=1$), the long-term regret rate converges to $\Theta\left(m^{1-r}\right)$; with imperfect learning ($p<1$), it converges to $\Theta\left(m^{1-r}\right)$ if $r\geq0.5$ but to $\Theta(\sqrt m)$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Offline data
nodes.statement: We assume that the decision-maker has access to $N_0=\gamma m^\beta+o\left(m^\beta\right)$ offline data points, with $\gamma>0$ and $\beta\in[0,1)$.

nodes.name: Regret with offline data
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma>0$ and $\beta\in[0,1)$ be defined such that $N_0=\gamma m^\beta+o\left(\gamma m^\beta\right)$. The optimal solution and the algorithm's solution achieve asymptotically tight regret rates with $N_0$ offline data points if $\delta = o\left(m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)-1}\right)$, equal to $c_0 \cdot \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma^{-\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)}$.
nodes.statement_short: With N_0 = gamma m^beta offline points, regret is Theta(m^{(1-beta)alpha_T(1-r)+beta(1-r)}).
nodes.label: thm:offline

nodes.name: Offline data acquisition cost
nodes.statement: We also consider a setting in which the decision-maker can acquire offline data at cost $c\leq1$ prior to committing to online facilities.

nodes.name: Offline acquisition decision A_0
nodes.statement: We add an initial decision $A_0$ corresponding to the number of offline data points acquired.

nodes.name: Regret with offline data acquisition
nodes.statement: With offline data acquisition, the optimal solution and the algorithm's solution achieve asymptotically tight regret rates if $\delta = o\left(m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}-1}\right)$, equal to $\left(c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot c^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot\alpha_T(1-r)\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}\cdot \left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: With costly offline data acquisition the regret rate is Theta(m^{(1-r)alpha_{T+1}}), as with T+1 online periods.
nodes.label: thm:warmstart

nodes.name: Adaptive re-optimization policy
nodes.statement: Assume that $\delta = o(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)-1})$. For $t=1,\cdots,T-1$, the adaptive solution opens $A^{\textsc{ad}}_t=\Theta(m^{\alpha_T(1-r^t)})$ facilities with a regret of $\Theta\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)$ as $m \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Adaptive re-optimization opens Theta(m^{alpha_T(1-r^t)}) facilities in early periods with the same Theta(m^{alpha_T(1-r)}) regret.
nodes.label: thm:adaptive

nodes.name: Facility-customer bipartite graph
nodes.statement: We formalize facility-customer interactions in a bipartite graph $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{A})$, where $\mathcal{F}=\{1, \cdots, n\}$ stores $n$ candidate facilities, $\mathcal{C}=\{1, \cdots, q\}$ stores $q$ customers, and $\mathcal{A}$ store undirected edges connecting facilities and customers.

nodes.name: Neighbourhoods C_i and F_j
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{C}_i=\left\{j\in\mathcal{C}\mid(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}\right\}$ the set of customers covered by facility $i\in\mathcal{F}$, and by $\mathcal{F}_j=\left\{i\in\mathcal{F}\mid(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}\right\}$ the set of facilities covering customer $j\in\mathcal{C}$.

nodes.name: Core model is a special case of the network model
nodes.statement: Our core model in Section~\ref{sec:base} is a special case with $|\mathcal{C}_i|=1$ for all $i$ and $|\mathcal{F}_j|=1$ for all $j$.

nodes.name: Customer coverage variables s_jt
Regret rate g(r)
nodes.statement:
We define $g(r)$ as the regret rate from Section~\ref{sec:base}, which we extend in this section.
\[g(r) = \begin{cases}
   	\alpha_T\cdot (1-r) & \text{if }p =1\\
   	\max\{\alpha_T\cdot (1-r),1/2\} & \text{if }p \neq 1
   \end{cases}\]

nodes.name: Central facilities and customers
nodes.statement: Let $\deg(\cdot)$ denote the degree function in $\mathcal{G}$. For $d>0$, we define central facilities $\mathcal{F}^{\textsc{ctl}}(d)=\{i\in\mathcal{F} \mid d< \deg(i)\}$ and central customers $\mathcal{C}^{\textsc{ctl}}(d)= \{j\in\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{F}^{\textsc{ctl}}(d)\cap\mathcal{F}_j\neq\emptyset\}$.

nodes.name: Degree
nodes.statement: There exist $d_\star$ and $k <g(r)$ such that: (i) $|\mathcal{C}^{\textsc{ctl}}(d_\star)|\leq \mathcal{O}(m^k)$; (ii) $\deg(j)\leq d_\star \;\;\forall j \in \mathcal{F}\setminus\mathcal{F}^{\textsc{ctl}}(d_\star)$; (iii) $\deg(j)\leq m^k,\ \forall j\in\mathcal{F}^{\textsc{ctl}}(d_\star)$; and (iv) $\deg(i)\leq d_\star \;\;\forall i \in \mathcal{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Few central customers (O(m^k), k<g(r)); all other facilities and all customers have degree at most d_star.

The online learning and optimization problem can therefore be formulated as follows:
\begin{align}
    \min_{\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{s}} \quad & \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it} \tag{$\mathcal{P}_N^*$}\\
    \text{s.t.}\quad&\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT} \geq m\right] \geq 1-\delta \nonumber\\

    \quad& y_{it}\in\{0,1\},\ \forall i\in \mathcal{F}, \ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber
\end{align}

nodes.statement: \caption{Algorithm to solve Problem~\eqref{prob:network}.}\small \begin{algorithmic} \item \textbf{Initialization:} $z^\dagger_{i0}=0,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{F}$. \item \textbf{Optimize.} Solve the following optimization problem. Record solution $y^\dagger_{it}$ for $i\in\mathcal{F}$ and $t=1,\cdots, T$. \begin{align} \min \quad & \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it} \tag{$\mathcal{P}_N^\dagger$}\\ \quad& \sum_{j=1}^q \left(1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p }{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} \sum_{i=1}^n y_{is} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y_{i\tau}}\right) \geq m+\Delta_G(m),\nonumber\\ \quad& y_{it}\in\{0,1\},\ \forall i\in \mathcal{F}, \ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber \end{align} \item Repeat, for $t=1,\cdots,T$: \begin{itemize} \item[] \textbf{Commit.} Observe $z_{it}\sim \mathrm{Ber}\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} \sum_{i=1}^n y_{is} +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$ for all $i\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $y^\dagger_{it}=1$. \item[] \textbf{Serve.} Update variables $s_{jt}=1$ for all $j\in\mathcal{C}_i$, $i\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $y^\dagger_{it}=1$. \end{itemize} \end{algorithmic}

nodes.name: Asymptotic optimality and sub-linear regret in the networked setting
nodes.statement: Consider a sequence of graphs $\mathcal{G}_1,\mathcal{G}_2,\cdots,\mathcal{G}_m,\cdots$ such that Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} admits a feasible solution with $\Omega(m^k)$ unopened facilities and unserved customers, with $0<k<g(r)$. Let $m^*(\varepsilon,T)$ and $m^{\textsc{L}}(T)$ be the solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:network} and the fully-learned solution. As $m \to \infty$, Algorithm~\ref{ALG_network} yields a feasible solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:network} and achieves a cost of $$m^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)\leq m^*(\varepsilon, T)+\begin{cases} o\left(m^{\alpha_T \cdot (1-r)}\right)& \text{if }p=1 \text{ or } (p \neq 1 \text{ and } \alpha_T\cdot(1-r)>1/2)\\ \mathcal{O}(m^{1/2}) & \text{if }p \neq 1\text{ and } \alpha_T\cdot(1-r)\leq 1/2 \end{cases}$$ Moreover, assume that $\delta = o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)$ and that $p=1$ or if the facilities of degree $d_\star$ can cover $\Omega(m)$ customers. Then the following holds: $m^*(\varepsilon, T)= m^{\textsc{L}}(T)+\Theta\left(m^{g(r)}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Algorithm 2 is asymptotically feasible and within o(m^{alpha_T(1-r)}) or O(sqrt m) of optimal; regret vs fully-learned is Theta(m^{g(r)}).
nodes.label: thm:network

nodes.name: Linear regret of the no-learning baseline (network)

nodes.name: Small-first structure of the algorithm's solution
nodes.statement: Let $y^\dagger_{it}$ be the solution of Algorithm~\ref{ALG_network} and $\pi_t(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)=\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} \sum_{i=1}^n y^\dagger_{is} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)$. Consider two facilities $i_1\neq i_2$ such that $y^\dagger_{i_1,t}=y^\dagger_{i_2, \tau}=1$ and $y^\dagger_{i_1,\tau}=y^\dagger_{i_2, t}=0$, with $t<\tau$. Then: \begin{align*} &\sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_1} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{i_2}}^q \prod_{\tau=1}^T \pi_t(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^\dagger_{iv}-\mathbf{1}\{v=t\}} \leq \sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{i_1}}^q \prod_{\tau=1}^T \pi_t(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^\dagger_{iv}-\mathbf{1}\{v=\tau\}} \end{align*} Similarly, if $y^\dagger_{i_2,\tau}=1$, $y^\dagger_{i_2,t}=0,\ \forall t\neq\tau$ and $y^\dagger_{i_1,t}=0,\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T$ then: \begin{align*} &\sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_1} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{i_2}}^q \prod_{\tau=1}^T \pi_t(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^\dagger_{iv}} \leq \sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{i_1}}^q \prod_{\tau=1}^T \pi_t(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^\dagger_{iv}-\mathbf{1}\{v=\tau\}} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Threshold solution in star graphs
nodes.statement: Assume that every customer is connected to one facility, i.e., $|\mathcal{F}_j|=1,\ \forall j\in\mathcal{C}$, and that every facility is opened at most once, i.e., $\sum_{t=1}^T y_{it}^\dagger \leq 1 \;\;\forall i$. Without loss of generality, arrange the set of facilities in increasing degree order (i.e. $\deg(i_1)\leq \deg(i_2)$ for all $i_1\leq i_2$). There exist $0\leq n_0\leq n_1 \leq \cdots \leq n_T=n$ such that the optimal solution $y_{it}^\dagger$ is of the form: \begin{align*} y_{it}=\begin{cases} 1 & n_{t-1}<i \leq n_{t} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Subproblem is a shortest path problem

nodes.name: Shortest-path construction
nodes.statement: The network representation, shown in Figure~\ref{fig:SP}, includes one source and a sink, and one node for each value of $n_t\in\{n_0,\cdots,n\}$ for each period $t\in\{1,\cdots,T-1\}$. For $t\leq T-2$, each node $n_t$ is connected to the nodes $n_{t+1}\geq n_t$, with an arc cost of $\sum_{i=n_{t-1}+1}^{n_t}\left(\frac{\varepsilon\deg(i)}{\left(n_{t}-n_0 +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$. Finally, each node $n_{T-1}$ is connected to the sink, with an arc cost of $\sum_{i=n_{T-1}+1}^{n}\left(\frac{\varepsilon\deg(i)}{\left(n-n_0 +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$. This shortest path problem can be solved in polynomial time in $n$, hence in polynomial time in $m$.

nodes.name: Algorithm 3: STAR, exact algorithm in star graphs
nodes.statement: \caption{Algorithm to solve Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} in star graph $\mathcal{G}$: \texttt{STAR}($\mathcal{G}$).}\small \begin{algorithmic}[1] \item \textbf{Initialization:} $\underline{n}_0=0,\overline{n}_0=n, n_0=\left\lfloor\frac{\overline{n}_0+\underline{n}_0}{2}\right\rfloor$. \item Iterate between Steps 1-3, until $\overline n_0-\underline n_0\leq 1$. \begin{itemize} \item[] \textbf{Step 1.} Solve Problem~\eqref{eq:SP} as a shortest path problem; retrieve solution $n_1^*(n_0),\cdots, n_{T-1}^*(n_0)$. \item[] \textbf{Step 2.} If $\displaystyle\sum_{i=n_0+1}^n \deg(i)-\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{i=n_{t-1}^*(n_0)+1}^{n_t}\left(\frac{\varepsilon \deg(i)}{\left(n_{t}^*(n_0)-n_0 +1\right)^r+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)}\right)\geq m+\Delta_G(m)$, update $\overline{n}_0 = n_0$; otherwise, update $\underline{n}_0 = n_0+1$. \item[] \textbf{Step 3.} Update $n_0 = \left\lfloor\frac{\overline{n}_0 + \underline{n}_0}{2}\right\rfloor$. \end{itemize} \item \textbf{Output:} Set $n_0^*\gets\overline{n}_0$; return $n-n_0^*$ as the optimal objective value of Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG}; use $n_0^*$, $n_1^*(n_0^*),\cdots, n_{T-1}^*(n_0^*)$ to reconstruct an optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} as given in Corollary~\ref{cor:small_first}. \end{algorithmic}

nodes.name: Weighted star-graph decomposition G_w
nodes.statement: This approach decomposes any bipartite graph $\mathcal{G}$ with maximum degree $d_\star$ into a weighted star graph $\mathcal{G}_w$ by duplicating every customer $j\in\mathcal{C}$ into $|\mathcal{F}_j|$ artificial customers---once per connected facility, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:graph_decompose}.

nodes.name: Connection weight w
nodes.statement: Thus, we weigh each connection in the star graph by $1/d_\star\leq w \leq 1$, so that each successful facility contributes a fraction $w$ per customer toward total coverage. The resulting problem is formulated as Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG}, except that the degree function is modified as $\text{deg}(i)=w|\mathcal{C}_i|$.

nodes.name: Algorithm 4: heuristic for general graphs
nodes.statement: \caption{Algorithm to solve Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} in a general graph $\mathcal{G}$.}\small \begin{algorithmic} \State Solve Problem~\eqref{eq:line} by line search; retrieve optimal solution $w^*$ and solution $\boldsymbol{y}^*\gets\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger(w^*)$. \State Repeat Steps 1 -2, until breaking condition is met. \begin{itemize} \item[] \textbf{Step 1.} Select $i_0\in\mathcal{F}$ and $t_0\in\mathcal{T}$ such that $y^*_{i_0,t_0}=1$. Define candidate solution $$\widetilde y_{it}^\dagger=\begin{cases} y_{it}^*&\text{for all $(i,t)\in\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{T}\setminus\{(i_0,t_0)\}$}\\ 0&\text{if $i=i_0$ and $t=t_0$} \end{cases}$$ \item[] \textbf{Step 2.} Update $y^*_{i_0,t_0}\gets0$ if the following condition is met. Otherwise, break. $$\sum_{j=1}^q \left(1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \widetilde y_{is}^\dagger +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} \widetilde y_{i\tau}^\dagger}\right) \geq m+\Delta_G(m)$$ \end{itemize} \item \textbf{Output:} $\boldsymbol{y}^*$ \end{algorithmic}

also_stated_at: Finally, we prune the resulting graph to further improve the solution. Let $w^*$ denote the optimal weight from Problem~\eqref{eq:line} and let $\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger(w^*)$ denote the corresponding optimal solution. We perform a greedy search to prune binary decisions $y_{it}^{\dagger}(w^*)$, by removing facilities one at a time as long as the coverage constraint in Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} is satisfied. The full algorithm is detailed in Algorithm \ref{alg:network_full}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (MLE concentration)
nodes.statement_short: Conditional independence lets standard MLE asymptotics apply; a sub-Gaussian concentration bound gives the rate.

nodes.name: Observations are conditionally independent, so MLE theory ap
nodes.statement: Per Equation~\eqref{eq:mle_estimation}, $\widehat{\theta}_t$ is the (conditional) maximum likelihood estimator based on independent, but not necessarily identically distributed, observations. While the facility success indicators $S_{it}$ may in general depend on prior facility openings, conditioning on the features $\bm{x}_i$ fixes the success probability $\eta_i = f_\theta(\bm{x}_i)$. As a result, the $S_{it}$ become conditionally independent across $i$. Since $y_{it}=1$ is chosen randomly with replacement among the set of facilities with $h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1$, this also implies that $y_{it}$ are conditionally independent across $i$ given $h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1$. In particular, this implies that $z_{it}$, determined by $S_{it}$ and $y_{it}$ to be conditionally independent fixing $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ and $h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$. This allows standard properties of maximum likelihood estimation to apply.
nodes.statement_short: Observations are conditionally independent, so MLE theory applies

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality and sub-Gaussian MLE concentration
nodes.statement:
Due to the regularity conditions in Assumption~\ref{ass:regularity}, we obtain the consistency of the estimator from the general theory of MLE estimation \citep[e.g.,][]{hoadley1971asymptotic}:
        $\sqrt{N_{t-1}}\left(\widehat{\theta}_t -\theta\right)\xrightarrow{d} N(0,\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ for some covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. Furthermore, $z_{is}$ is Bernoulli, hence sub-Gaussian. By concentration inequality of sub-Gaussian maximum likelihood estimators \citep[see e.g.][]{yang2024concentration}, we have:
        \[\mathbb{P}(\|\widehat{\theta}_t-\theta\|_2>\varepsilon)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\varepsilon^2N_{t-1}}{C}\right)\]
        where $C$ is an absolute constant.
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic normality and sub-Gaussian MLE concentration

nodes.name: Classification accuracy bound
nodes.statement: The following holds: \[\left|\mathbb{P}\left(S_{it}=1 \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1\right)- \mathbb{P}\left(S_{it}=1 \mid h^*(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1\right)\right|\leq\mathbb{P}\left( \left|f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - \frac{1}{2}\right| < \varepsilon \right) + \mathbb{P}\left( \left|f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)\right| > \varepsilon \right)\]

nodes.label: lem:bound_classification

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (classification accuracy)
nodes.statement:
The result is derived as follows, where $p_X(\cdot)$ denotes the probability distribution function of $\mathcal{Q}$ (Assumption~\ref{ass:sampling}):
\begin{align*}
& \left|\mathbb{P}\left(S_{it}=1 \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1\right)- \mathbb{P}\left(S_{it}=1 \mid h^*(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1\right)\right|\\
=& \left| \int_{f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) > \frac{1}{2}} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x 
     - \int_{f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) > \frac{1}{2}} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x \right| \\
=& \left| \int_{f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) > \frac{1}{2}, f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) < \frac{1}{2}} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x + \int_{f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) < \frac{1}{2}, f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) > \frac{1}{2}} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x \right| \\
\leq& \left| \int_{f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) > \frac{1}{2}, f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) < \frac{1}{2} - \varepsilon} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x +\int_{f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) < \frac{1}{2}, f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) > \frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x + \int_{\left|f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - \frac{1}{2}\right| < \varepsilon} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x \right| \\
\leq& \left| \int_{\left|f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - \frac{1}{2}\right| < \varepsilon} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x \right| + \left| \int_{\left|f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)\right| > \varepsilon} f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) p_X(\boldsymbol{x}_i) \, \mathrm{d} x \right| \\
\leq& \mathbb{P}\left( \left|f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - \frac{1}{2}\right| < \varepsilon \right)
    + \mathbb{P}\left( \left|f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)\right| > \varepsilon \right).
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Law of total probability and Lemma bound_classification give
nodes.statement:
Now define $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that $\frac{C\varepsilon_0^\alpha}{3^\alpha}=\frac{\varepsilon}{3}$. We proceed to prove the main result:
\begin{align*}
1-\mu_t=&\mathbb{P}(S_{it}=1 \mid y_{i1}=\cdots=y_{i1,t-1}=0\ ;\ h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)\\
=&\frac{\mathbb{P}(S_{it}=1 \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)-\mathbb{P}(y_{i\tau}=1\ \text{for $\tau\leq t-1$} \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)\mathbb{P}(S_{it}=1 \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1, y_{i\tau}=1\ \text{for $\tau\leq t-1$})}{\mathbb{P}(y_{i1}=\cdots=y_{i1,t-1}=0 \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)}\\
\geq& \mathbb{P}(S_{it}=1 \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)-\mathbb{P}(y_{i\tau}=1\ \text{for $\tau\leq t-1$} \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)\\
\geq&\mathbb{P}(S_{it}=1 \mid h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)-\frac{\varepsilon}{3(N_{t-1})^{1/2-\gamma}}\\
\geq&\mathbb{P}(S_{it}=1 \mid h^*(\boldsymbol{x}_i)=1)-\frac{\varepsilon}{3(N_{t-1})^{1/2-\gamma}}- \mathbb{P}\left( \left|f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - \frac{1}{2}\right| < \frac{\varepsilon_0}{3(N_{t-1})^{1/2-\gamma}} \right)\\
    &-\mathbb{P}\left( \left|f_{\widehat\theta_t}(\boldsymbol{x}_i) - f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)\right| > \frac{\varepsilon_0}{3(N_{t-1})^{1/2-\gamma}} \right),
\end{align*}
where the equality comes from the law of total probabilities, the first inequality is obtained by lower bounding probabilities by 1, the second inequality follows from Equation~\eqref{eq:regime}, and the third inequality is derived from Lemma~\ref{lem:bound_classification}.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary (Learning environment)
nodes.statement:
Define $\widetilde\mu_t$ such that $\widetilde{S}_{it} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(1-\widetilde\mu_t)$. Per Proposition \ref{prop:MLE}, $\widetilde\mu_t\geq  \mu_t$, irregardless of the possible dependence of $\mu_t$ on the previous set of selected facilities. Since $B_t \mid \mu_t \sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A_t, 1-\mu_t\right)$ and $\widetilde{B}_t \sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A_t, 1-\widetilde\mu_t\right)$, this implies:
    \[\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\widetilde{B}_t\geq m \right] \leq \mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^TB_t\geq m \mid \mu_t \right]\]
Therefore, by the law of total expectation, taking the expectation over $\mu_t$ gives:
    \[\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\widetilde{B}_t\geq m \right] \leq \mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^TB_t\geq m \right]\]

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary (Success Distribution)
nodes.statement:
Recall that $B_t \;=\; \sum_{i:\,y_{it}=1} S_{it}$. Under Assumption~\ref{ass:sampling} the indices with $y_{it}=1$ are drawn
\emph{with} replacement from the set
$\mathcal{J}_t$. Therefore, Assumption~\ref{ass:classification} implies that every draw from
$\mathcal{J}_t$ has the same conditional success probability
\[
  p_t \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_t|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{J}_t} \eta_i = \mathbb{P}(h_t(\boldsymbol{x}_i) = S_{it} \mid i \in \mathcal{J}_t)=1-\frac{\varepsilon p}{(N_{t-1}+1)^{r}}-\varepsilon\,(1-p),
\]
so that $S_{it} \mid y_{it} = 1 \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_t)$ for all $i\in\mathcal{J}_t$.
The model specification $S_{it} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\eta_i)$ further
assumes independence across facilities, i.e.\ $S_{it}\;\perp \!\!\! \perp\;S_{jt}$ for
$i\neq j$.
Because sampling is with replacement, the selection indicators
$\{y_{it}\}_{i\in\mathcal{J}_t}$ are independent conditional on $i \in \mathcal{J}_t$ as well; hence, conditional on
$\mathcal{J}_t$, the random variables
$\{S_{it}:y_{it}=1\}$ are i.i.d.\ $\text{Bernoulli}(p_t)$.
Therefore
\[
  B_t \;\sim\; \text{Binomial}\bigl(A_t,\,p_t\bigr),
\]
which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: With-replacement sampling and the learning function make the successes i.i.d. Bernoulli(p_t), so B_t is binomial.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (main)
nodes.statement_short: Combine the deterministic solution (Lemma main_det), feasibility of Algorithm 1 (Lemma main_feasible) and the lower bound (Lemma main_lower).

nodes.name: Notation for stochastic, algorithmic and deterministic solut
nodes.statement: Throughout this proof, we denote by $A^*_{t}$ the optimal solution of the stochastic problem (Problem~\eqref{prob:main}), by $A^\dagger_{t}$ the solution of Algorithm~\ref{ALG}, and by $A^{\textsc{D}}_{t}$ the solution of the deterministic approximation (Problem~\eqref{prob:main_det}). We denote by $B^*_{t}$, $B^\dagger_{t}$, and $B^{\textsc{D}}_{t}$ the corresponding numbers of facilities successfully opened \emph{at} period $t$, and by $N^*_{t}$, $N^\dagger_{t}$, and $N^{\textsc{D}}_{t}$ the corresponding number of facilities successfully opened \emph{by} period $t$. The optimal values are denoted as $m^*(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_{t}$, $m^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1}^T A^\dagger_{t}$, and $m^{\textsc{D}}(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1}^T A^{\textsc{D}}_{t}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for stochastic, algorithmic and deterministic solutions

nodes.name: Proof plan via three lemmas
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:main_det} elicits the solution $A^{\textsc{D}}_{t}$; Lemma~\ref{lem:main_feasible} establishes the feasibility of solution $A^\dagger_{t}$ in view of the chance constraint in Problem~\eqref{prob:main}, thus providing a constructive upper bound of $m^*(\varepsilon, T)$; and Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lower} provides a lower bound of $m^*(\varepsilon, T)$. Throughout the proof, we will focus on the case where $r\neq 1$. The case where $r=1$ is treated identically.
nodes.statement_short: Proof plan via three lemmas; focus on r != 1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (asymptotic solution of P^D)
nodes.statement:
Note that the constraint $N^D_T\geq m$ is binding at optimality, so the problem can be re-written as:
\begin{align*}
    \min\ \left\{\ \sum_{t=1}^T A^D_t \ \ \bigg|\ \ \sum_{t=1}^TA^D_t \left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r} - \varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\ \right)=m\right\}
\end{align*}

Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ be the dual variable associated with the equality constraint. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions yield the following vanishing gradient equation:
$$1+\lambda\left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r} - \varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)+\lambda\sum_{\tau=t+1}^T\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot r\cdot A^D_\tau}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}=0,\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}$$

Clearly, $\lambda\neq0$. After re-arranging the terms, we obtain:
$$\frac{1}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r}-\sum_{\tau=t+1}^T\frac{r\cdot A^D_\tau}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}=\frac{1+\lambda}{p\lambda\varepsilon} - \frac{1-p}{p},\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}$$

Note that this expression is independent of $t$. Therefore, for all $t=1,\cdots,T-1$, we have:
$$\frac{1}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r}-\sum_{\tau=t+1}^T\frac{ r\cdot A^D_\tau}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}=\frac{1}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t} A^D_s +1\right)^r}-\sum_{\tau=t+2}^T\frac{r\cdot A^D_\tau}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}.$$

This system of equations gives rise to a simple recurrence relation for $A^D_{t}$:
\begin{equation*}
    A^D_{t+1} = \frac{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}{r\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t} A^D_s +1\right),\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T-1.
\end{equation*}

Let us define $u_t = \sum_{s=1}^t A^D_s + 1$. By expressing $A^D_t=u_t-u_{t-1}$, we can re-write the recursion as:
\begin{equation*}
    u_{t+1} - u_t = \frac{u_t^{r+1}}{ru_{t-1}^r}-\frac{u_t}{r},\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T-1,
\end{equation*}
i.e., as:
\begin{equation}
    u_{t+1} + \left(\frac{1}{r}-1\right)u_t = \frac{u_t^{r+1}}{ru_{t-1}^r},\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T-1. \end{equation}

We are interested in the behavior of $u_t$ as $m \to \infty$. We perform a leading-order analysis and a leading-coefficient analysis, assuming that $u_t = \Theta(g(t)m^{f(t)})$. Note, first, that the boundary condition of $u_0=1=\Theta(1)$ implies that $g(0)=1$ and $f(0)=0$. Moreover, we prove that $u_T = \frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon} + o(m)=\Theta(m)$, so that $g(T)=c_0$ and $f(T)=1$. Indeed, consider the solution $\bar A_1=\frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon}$ and $\bar A_2=\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon} $. We have:
\begin{align*}
    N^D_2 &=  \bar A_1(1-\varepsilon)+\bar A_2\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{(\bar A_1+1)^{r}}-(1-p)\varepsilon\right)\\
    \geq& m^{1/(r+1)} + m - \frac{m}{(\bar A_1+1)^{r}}\\
    \geq& m^{1/(r+1)}+m-\frac{m}{m^{r/(r+1)}}\\
    =& m
\end{align*}
Therefore, $\left(\frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon},\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon},0,\cdots,0\right)$ is a feasible solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main_det} with $T\geq2$, so
$$\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon}\leq u_T\leq \frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon}+\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon}+1$$
This proves that $u_T = \frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon} + o(m)=\Theta(m)$, hence $g(T)=c_0$ and $f(T)=1$.



Let us derive the expression of $f(t)$. From Equation~\eqref{eq:recur_rel}, we obtain the following recursion:
\[f(t+1) = (r+1)f(t)-rf(t-1),\]
i.e.:
\[f(t+1)-f(t) = r\left(f(t)-f(t-1)\right).\]
We derive:
$$f(t+1)-f(t)=Kr^t,\quad\text{where $K=f(1)-f(0)=f(1)$.}$$
By summation and by telescoping the sum, this yields:
$$\sum_{s=0}^{T-1}(f(s+1)-f(s))=f(T)-f(0)=\frac{K}{1-r}\left(1-r^T\right).$$
From the boundary conditions, we have $f(T)-f(0)=1$, so that:
$$f(t+1)-f(t)=r^{t}\cdot\frac{1-r}{1-r^T}$$
Again, by summation and by telescoping the sum, the following holds:
$$f(t)=\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}(f(s+1)-f(s))=\frac{1-r}{1-r^T}\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}r^s=\alpha_T(1-r^t).$$
In conclusion, the leading-order analysis leads to:
$$u_t=\Theta\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r^t)}\right)=\Theta\left(m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right)}\right).$$

We conduct a similar analysis for the leading coefficient of $u_t$. Equation~\eqref{eq:recur_rel} yields
\[g(t+1) = \frac{g(t)^{1+r}}{r(g(t-1))^r}\]
Define $h(t)=\log g(t)$ and we have the following recurrent relation with $h(0)=h(T)=0$:
\[h(t+1) = (r+1)h(t)-rh(t-1)-\log r\]
We proceed as above, with the added drift term. We derive:
\begin{align*}
    & h(t+1)-h(t) = r\left(h(t)-h(t-1)\right)-\log(r)\\
    & h(t+1)-h(t)=Kr^t-\log r\cdot\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}r^s=K'r^t-\frac{1}{1-r}\log r,\quad\text{where $K=h(1)-h(0)$ and $K'=K+\frac{\log r}{1-r}$.}\\
    & \sum_{s=0}^{T-1}(h(s+1)-h(s))=\underbrace{h(T)-h(0)}_{=\log(c_0}=K'\frac{\left(1-r^T\right)}{1-r}-\frac{T\log r}{1-r}\implies K'=\frac{T\log r}{1-r^T} + \frac{\log(c_0)(1-r)}{1-r^T}\\
    & h(t+1)-h(t)=\left(\frac{T\log r}{1-r^T} + \frac{\log(c_0)(1-r)}{1-r^T}\right)r^t -\frac{\log r}{1-r} \\
    & h(t)=\frac{-\log r}{1-r}\left(t-T\alpha_T(1-r^t)\right)+\log(c_0)\cdot\alpha_T(1-r^t).
\end{align*}
Bringing the two results together, we obtain:
\begin{align*}
    u_t&=r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right)}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right)}\right)
\end{align*}
For ease of the exposition, let us write $u_t=r^{-\frac{\overline{h}(t)}{1-r}}c_0^{f(t)}m^{f(t)} + o\left(m^{f(t)}\right)$. Note that:
\begin{align}
    \overline{h}(t)-r\overline{h}(t-1)&=\left(t-T\alpha_T(1-r^t)\right)-r\left(t-1-T\alpha_T(1-r^{t-1})\right)
    =(1-r)t+r-\frac{T(1-r)}{1-r^T} \\
    f(t)-rf(t-1)&=\alpha_T(1-r^t)-r\cdot\alpha_T(1-r^{t-1})
    =\alpha_T\cdot(1-r) \end{align}

We conclude as follows:
\begin{align*}
   \left(1-(1-p)\varepsilon)\right)\sum_{t=1}^T A^D_t &= m + \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{A^D_t \cdot\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r}\\
   &=  m + \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot(u_t-u_{t-1})}{u^r_{t-1}}\\
   &= m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot  \sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{\overline{h}(t)-r\overline{h}(t-1)}{1-r}}\cdot c_0^{f(t)-rf(t-1)}\cdot m^{f(t)-rf(t-1)}+o\left(m^{f(t)-rf(t-1)}\right)\\
   &= m +\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\left(\sum_{t=1}^T \frac{1}{r^t}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^{\frac{r}{1-r}}\cdot r^{T\cdot\alpha_T}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\\
   &= m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right),
\end{align*}
where the fourth equality follows from Equations~\eqref{eq:hbar_rec} and~\eqref{eq:alpha_rec}. The expressions for $A^D_t$ follow immediately from the expression of $u_t$ and the fact that $A^D_t=u_t-u_{t-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: KKT conditions give a recurrence for cumulative openings u_t; leading-order and leading-coefficient analyses solve it. Key step: exponents satisfy f(t+1)-f(t)=r(f(t)-f(t-1)).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma main_det (Section 9.1)
nodes.statement:
Note that the constraint $N^D_T\geq m$ is binding at optimality, so the problem can be re-written as:
\begin{align*}
    \min\ \left\{\ \sum_{t=1}^T A^D_t \ \ \bigg|\ \ \sum_{t=1}^TA^D_t \left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r} - \varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\ \right)=m\right\}

$$\frac{1}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r}-\sum_{\tau=t+1}^T\frac{ r\cdot A^D_\tau}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}=\frac{1}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t} A^D_s +1\right)^r}-\sum_{\tau=t+2}^T\frac{r\cdot A^D_\tau}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}.$$

\begin{equation*}
    A^D_{t+1} = \frac{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}{r\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t} A^D_s +1\right),\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T-1.
\end{equation*}

Let us define $u_t = \sum_{s=1}^t A^D_s + 1$. By expressing $A^D_t=u_t-u_{t-1}$, we can re-write the recursion as:
\begin{equation*}
    u_{t+1} - u_t = \frac{u_t^{r+1}}{ru_{t-1}^r}-\frac{u_t}{r},\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T-1,
\end{equation*}
i.e., as:
\begin{equation}
    u_{t+1} + \left(\frac{1}{r}-1\right)u_t = \frac{u_t^{r+1}}{ru_{t-1}^r},\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T-1. \end{equation}

We are interested in the behavior of $u_t$ as $m \to \infty$. We perform a leading-order analysis and a leading-coefficient analysis, assuming that $u_t = \Theta(g(t)m^{f(t)})$. Note, first, that the boundary condition of $u_0=1=\Theta(1)$ implies that $g(0)=1$ and $f(0)=0$. \begin{align*}
    N^D_2 &=  \bar A_1(1-\varepsilon)+\bar A_2\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{(\bar A_1+1)^{r}}-(1-p)\varepsilon\right)\\
    \geq& m^{1/(r+1)} + m - \frac{m}{(\bar A_1+1)^{r}}\\
    \geq& m^{1/(r+1)}+m-\frac{m}{m^{r/(r+1)}}\\
    =& m
\end{align*}
Therefore, $\left(\frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon},\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon},0,\cdots,0\right)$ is a feasible solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main_det} with $T\geq2$, so
$$\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon}\leq u_T\leq \frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon}+\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon}+1$$
This proves that $u_T = \frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon} + o(m)=\Theta(m)$, hence $g(T)=c_0$ and $f(T)=1$.



Let us derive the expression of $f(t)$. From Equation~\eqref{eq:recur_rel}, we obtain the following recursion:
\[f(t+1) = (r+1)f(t)-rf(t-1),\]
i.e.:
\[f(t+1)-f(t) = r\left(f(t)-f(t-1)\right).\]
We derive:
$$f(t+1)-f(t)=Kr^t,\quad\text{where $K=f(1)-f(0)=f(1)$.}$$
By summation and by telescoping the sum, this yields:
$$\sum_{s=0}^{T-1}(f(s+1)-f(s))=f(T)-f(0)=\frac{K}{1-r}\left(1-r^T\right).$$
From the boundary conditions, we have $f(T)-f(0)=1$, so that:
$$f(t+1)-f(t)=r^{t}\cdot\frac{1-r}{1-r^T}$$
Again, by summation and by telescoping the sum, the following holds:
$$f(t)=\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}(f(s+1)-f(s))=\frac{1-r}{1-r^T}\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}r^s=\alpha_T(1-r^t).$$
In conclusion, the leading-order analysis leads to:
$$u_t=\Theta\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r^t)}\right)=\Theta\left(m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right)}\right).$$

We conduct a similar analysis for the leading coefficient of $u_t$. Equation~\eqref{eq:recur_rel} yields
\[g(t+1) = \frac{g(t)^{1+r}}{r(g(t-1))^r}\]
Define $h(t)=\log g(t)$ and we have the following recurrent relation with $h(0)=h(T)=0$:
\[h(t+1) = (r+1)h(t)-rh(t-1)-\log r\]
We proceed as above, with the added drift term. We derive:
\begin{align*}
    & h(t+1)-h(t) = r\left(h(t)-h(t-1)\right)-\log(r)\\
    & h(t+1)-h(t)=Kr^t-\log r\cdot\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}r^s=K'r^t-\frac{1}{1-r}\log r,\quad\text{where $K=h(1)-h(0)$ and $K'=K+\frac{\log r}{1-r}$.}\\
    & \sum_{s=0}^{T-1}(h(s+1)-h(s))=\underbrace{h(T)-h(0)}_{=\log(c_0}=K'\frac{\left(1-r^T\right)}{1-r}-\frac{T\log r}{1-r}\implies K'=\frac{T\log r}{1-r^T} + \frac{\log(c_0)(1-r)}{1-r^T}\\
    & h(t+1)-h(t)=\left(\frac{T\log r}{1-r^T} + \frac{\log(c_0)(1-r)}{1-r^T}\right)r^t -\frac{\log r}{1-r} \\
    & h(t)=\frac{-\log r}{1-r}\left(t-T\alpha_T(1-r^t)\right)+\log(c_0)\cdot\alpha_T(1-r^t).
\end{align*}
Bringing the two results together, we obtain:
\begin{align*}
    u_t&=r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right)}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right)}\right)
\end{align*}
For ease of the exposition, let us write $u_t=r^{-\frac{\overline{h}(t)}{1-r}}c_0^{f(t)}m^{f(t)} + o\left(m^{f(t)}\right)$. Note that:
\begin{align}
    \overline{h}(t)-r\overline{h}(t-1)&=\left(t-T\alpha_T(1-r^t)\right)-r\left(t-1-T\alpha_T(1-r^{t-1})\right)
    =(1-r)t+r-\frac{T(1-r)}{1-r^T} \\
    f(t)-rf(t-1)&=\alpha_T(1-r^t)-r\cdot\alpha_T(1-r^{t-1})
    =\alpha_T\cdot(1-r) \end{align}

We conclude as follows:
\begin{align*}
   \left(1-(1-p)\varepsilon)\right)\sum_{t=1}^T A^D_t &= m + \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{A^D_t \cdot\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r}\\
   &=  m + \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot(u_t-u_{t-1})}{u^r_{t-1}}\\
   &= m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot  \sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{\overline{h}(t)-r\overline{h}(t-1)}{1-r}}\cdot c_0^{f(t)-rf(t-1)}\cdot m^{f(t)-rf(t-1)}+o\left(m^{f(t)-rf(t-1)}\right)\\
   &= m +\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\left(\sum_{t=1}^T \frac{1}{r^t}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^{\frac{r}{1-r}}\cdot r^{T\cdot\alpha_T}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\\
   &= m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right),
\end{align*}
where the fourth equality follows from Equations~\eqref{eq:hbar_rec} and~\eqref{eq:alpha_rec}. The expressions for $A^D_t$ follow immediately from the expression of $u_t$ and the fact that $A^D_t=u_t-u_{t-1}$.

nodes.name: KKT stationarity with dual variable lambda
nodes.statement:
Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ be the dual variable associated with the equality constraint. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions yield the following vanishing gradient equation:
$$1+\lambda\left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r} - \varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)+\lambda\sum_{\tau=t+1}^T\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot r\cdot A^D_\tau}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1} A^D_s +1\right)^{r+1}}=0,\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}$$

nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Claim: u_T ~ c_0 m (boundary condition at T)
nodes.statement:
Moreover, we prove that $u_T = \frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon} + o(m)=\Theta(m)$, so that $g(T)=c_0$ and $f(T)=1$. Indeed, consider the solution $\bar A_1=\frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon}$ and $\bar A_2=\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon} $. We have:
\begin{align*}
    N^D_2 &=  \bar A_1(1-\varepsilon)+\bar A_2\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{(\bar A_1+1)^{r}}-(1-p)\varepsilon\right)\\
    \geq& m^{1/(r+1)} + m - \frac{m}{(\bar A_1+1)^{r}}\\
    \geq& m^{1/(r+1)}+m-\frac{m}{m^{r/(r+1)}}\\
    =& m
\end{align*}
Therefore, $\left(\frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon},\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon},0,\cdots,0\right)$ is a feasible solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main_det} with $T\geq2$, so
$$\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon}\leq u_T\leq \frac{m^{1/(r+1)}}{1-\varepsilon}+\frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon}+1$$
This proves that $u_T = \frac{m}{1-(1-p)\varepsilon} + o(m)=\Theta(m)$, hence $g(T)=c_0$ and $f(T)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: u_T ~ c_0 m (boundary condition at T)

Let us derive the expression of $f(t)$. From Equation~\eqref{eq:recur_rel}, we obtain the following recursion:
\[f(t+1) = (r+1)f(t)-rf(t-1),\]
i.e.:
\[f(t+1)-f(t) = r\left(f(t)-f(t-1)\right).\]

where the fourth equality follows from Equations~\eqref{eq:hbar_rec} and~\eqref{eq:alpha_rec}. The expressions for $A^D_t$ follow immediately from the expression of $u_t$ and the fact that $A^D_t=u_t-u_{t-1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Remark (order of l)
nodes.statement:
Per Lemma \ref{lem:main_det}, we have:
\[\sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}= c_0\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + o\left(m^{\alpha_T \cdot (1-r)}\right)\right) \]

\[\sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\geq c_0\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right) \]

The derivative of the last term of the left-hand side with respect to $m$ is equal to $c_0$, so the derivative of the left-hand side is at least equal to $c_0$. Therefore, for $m$ large enough:
\begin{align*}
    & \sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot (m+\Delta(m))^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\geq c_0\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \Delta(m)\right)\\
    & \sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot \left(m-m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\leq c_0\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} \right)
\end{align*}

This implies that $\ell \leq m + \Delta(m)$ and $\ell\geq m-m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of the allocation sum in l (derivative at least c_0) sandwiches l between m - m^{alpha_T(1-r)} and m + Delta(m).

\[\sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\geq c_0\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right) \]

The derivative of the last term of the left-hand side with respect to $m$ is equal to $c_0$, so the derivative of the left-hand side is at least equal to $c_0$. Therefore, for $m$ large enough:
\begin{align*}
    & \sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot (m+\Delta(m))^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\geq c_0\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \Delta(m)\right)\\
    & \sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot \left(m-m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\leq c_0\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} \right)
\end{align*}

This implies that $\ell \leq m + \Delta(m)$ and $\ell\geq m-m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}$.

nodes.name: Hoeffding's inequality on total successes
nodes.statement:
Note that $0\leq B^\dagger_t\leq A^\dagger_t$ for all $t=1,\cdots,T$. By Hoeffding's inequality, we have:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(N^\dagger_T<m\right)
    &=\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t\right]-\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t < \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t\right] - m\right)\\
    &\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t - \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t\right]\right|>\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t\right]-m\right|\right)\\
    &\leq2 \exp\left(-2\frac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t\right]-m\right)^2}{\sum_{t=1}^T A^\dagger_t}\right)
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Hoeffding's inequality on total successes

Similarly, we can also prove that:
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^\dagger_t\right)
    = &\sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{Var}(B^\dagger_t)\\
    \geq&\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^T A^\dagger_t \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^\dagger_s +1\right)^r}
    \\
    = &\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^T   \frac{\varepsilon r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot \ell^{\alpha_T(1-r^t)}}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(s-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^s)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^s)}\cdot \ell^{\alpha_T(1-r^s)}  +1\right)^r}\\
    \geq & \frac{1}{2}   \frac{\varepsilon c_0 \ell}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{T-1} r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(s-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^s)\right)}\cdot c_0^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^s)}\cdot \ell^{\alpha_T(1-r^s)}  +1\right)^r}\\
    =& \frac{1}{2}   \frac{\varepsilon c_0 \ell}{c_0^r\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p \cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T \cdot(1-r)}+\Delta(m)-\ell\right)^r}\\
    \geq& \frac{1}{2}   \frac{\varepsilon c_0 \left(m-m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)}{c_0^r\left(m+\varepsilon\cdot p \cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T \cdot(1-r)}+\Delta(m)-\left(m-m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)\right)^r}\\
    =& \Omega(m^{1-\alpha_T \cdot r(1-r)}),
\end{align*}
where the last inequality comes from Remark~\ref{rem:lm}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (lower bound)
nodes.statement:
\underline{Case 1: $p=1$.}

Let $k$ be such that $\frac{1}{2}\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)<k<\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)$. Let us define the following ``good'' event:
$$\mathcal{E}=\left\{\left|B_t - A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\right|\leq m^k,\ \forall t \in \{1,\cdots, T\}\right\}$$

\begin{lemma} If $A_t\leq m+ \mathcal{O}(m^{\alpha_T \cdot (1-r)})$ for all $t=1,\cdots, T$, then $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^c) =\mathcal{O}(\exp\left(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right))$ as $m \to \infty$.
\end{lemma}
\proof{Proof:}
    By construction, $\mathbb{E}[B_t] = A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\leq A_t$. From Bernstein's inequality, using the definition of $B_t=\sum_{i:y_{it}=1}S_{it}$:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{P}(|B_t - \mathbb{E}[B_t]| \geq m^k)
        &\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{1/2\cdot m^{2k}}{\sum_{i:y_{it}=1}\text{Var}(S_{it})+1/3\cdot m^k}\right)\\
        &= 2\exp\left(-\frac{1/2\cdot m^{2k}}{\text{Var}(B_t)+1/3\cdot m^k}\right)\\
        &\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{m^{2k}}{4\varepsilon \zeta_T m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + 2m^k/3}\right)\\
        &= \mathcal{O}\left(\exp\left(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right),
    \end{align*}
    where the equality follows from the independence of $B_1,\cdots,B_T$ and the second inequality uses the lower bound on the variance term from the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:main_feasible}. By assumption, $2k - \alpha_T\cdot(1-r) > 0$, so $\mathbb{P}\left(|B_t - \mathbb{E}[B_t]| \geq m^k\right) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. We obtain from the union bound:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^c)
    &=\mathbb{P}\left(\exists t \in \{1,\cdots, T\} \;\; : \;\; \left|B_t - A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\right|\geq m^k\right)\\
    &\leq \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{P}\left(\left|B_t - A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\right|\geq m^k\right)\\
    & =\mathcal{O}(\exp\left(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right))
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding_bound}.\hfill\Halmos\endproof

\begin{lemma} Let $(B^*_1,\cdots,B^*_T)$ be a solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. If $\delta = o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)$, then as $m \to \infty$:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty \sigma \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*=\sigma \mid \mathcal{E}\right) & \geq m + o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\\
    \sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty(\sigma-Tm^k)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E} \right)&\geq m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\proof{Proof:}
Note that the optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main} must satisfy the constraint:
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*\geq m\right)\geq 1-\delta = 1-o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right) \end{equation}
From the law of total probabilities, we obtain, using Equation~\eqref{eq:Bmdelta} and Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding_bound}:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*\geq m \mid \mathcal{E}\right)
    &=\frac{\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*\geq m\right)-\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*\geq m\mid \mathcal{E}^c \right)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^c)}{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})}\\
    &\geq1-o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)-\mathcal{O}\left(\exp\left(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\\
    &=1-o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)
\end{align*}
Then, we have:
\begin{equation*}
    \sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty \sigma \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*=\sigma \mid \mathcal{E}\right)\geq m\cdot \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*\geq m \mid \mathcal{E}\right)\geq m+o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)
\end{equation*}

Similarly:
\begin{align*}
    &\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty(\sigma-Tm^k)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*
    =\sigma\mid \mathcal{E} \right)\\
    &\geq (m-Tm^k)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*\geq m\mid \mathcal{E} \right)\\
    &= m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}(1-Tm^{k-1})^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\left(1-o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)\right)\\
    &= m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\left(1-T^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}m^{(k-1)\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+o\left(m^{(k-1)\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\left(1-o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)\right)\\
    &=m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+o(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}),
\end{align*}
where the first equality results from Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding_bound}, the second equality follows from Taylor expansion and the last equality follows from the assumption that $k<\alpha_T(1-r)\leq1$.
This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:sum_bound}.\hfill\Halmos

Now, let $(A^*_1,\cdots,A^*_T)$ and $(B^*_1,\cdots,B^*_T)$ denote the optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. We obtain from Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding_bound}:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t\right]
    &=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}\right]\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})+\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}^c\right]\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^c)\\
    &\geq \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}\right]\left(1-\mathcal{O}(\exp(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}))\right)\\
    &=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}\right] + o(1)
\end{align*}

Conditioned on $\mathcal{E}$, we have:
$$\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\left|\sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}(B^*_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T (B^*_t-\mathbb{E}(B^*_t))\right|\leq\sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}(B^*_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T |B^*_t-\mathbb{E}(B^*_t)|\leq\sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}(B^*_t)+Tm^k$$

Therefore, the following holds:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t\mid \mathcal{E}\right]
    &=\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}, \sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\right]\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma \mid \mathcal{E} \right)\\
    &=\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}, \sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma, \sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \left(1- \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^*_s +1\right)^r}\right)\geq \sigma-Tm^k\right]\\&\qquad\qquad\cdot\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E} \right)
\end{align*}
The first expression resembles the deterministic variant of the full problem, with a right-hand side target of $\sigma-Tm^k$. From Lemma~\ref{lem:main_det}, we can lower bound it to obtain:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t\mid \mathcal{E}\right]
    &\geq c_0\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty\left(\sigma-Tm^k+\varepsilon\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \left(\sigma-Tm^k\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ o\left(\left(\sigma-Tm^k\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E}\right)\\
    &+ o(1)\\
    &\geq c_0\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty\sigma\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E}\right)+c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot\zeta_T\cdot\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty(\sigma-Tm^k)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E}\right)\\
    &+ o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\quad\text{(because $k<\alpha_T(1-r)$)}\\
    &\geq c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)
    \quad\text{(Lemma~\ref{lem:sum_bound})}
\end{align*}
The proof is completed since $\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t\right]\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}\right] + o(1)$. 

\underline{Case 2: $p\neq 1$.}

First, we could follow the same logic as in the proof for $p=1$, and get:
\[m^*(\varepsilon,T) \geq c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\]

This bound is tight if $\alpha_T(1-r)\geq1/2$, since the upper-bounding solution admits a buffer of $\Theta(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)})$ in that case; however, if $\alpha_T(1-r)<1/2$, the bound may no longer be tight since the the upper-bounding buffer then grows in $\Theta(\sqrt{m})$. To improve it, we assume by contradiction that:
\[m^*(\varepsilon,T)=\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t <c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)\]
Consider independent trials $S'_{it} \sim \mathrm{Bern}\left(1-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$ and define $B'_t = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}_t} S'_{it}$. We have:
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t \geq m\right)\leq \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \geq m\right)\]
Then by the Berry-Esseen Theorem, we have:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t<m \right)
    =&\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t -\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \right] <m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p)) \right)
    \\=&\Phi\left(\frac{m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)}}\right) + \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\sum_{t=1}^TA^*_t(1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)(2\varepsilon(1-p)-1)}{\left(\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)\right)^{3/2}}\right)
    \\=&\Phi\left(\frac{m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)}}\right) + o(1)
\end{align*}
We use the contradiction assumption $\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t < c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)$ to bound the numerator and the fact that $\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t<2c_0m$ to bound the denominator. We obtain
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t<m \right)> &\Phi\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}}{\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}}\right) + o(1)   =\delta +o(1)
\end{align*}
Therefore, for sufficiently large $m$:
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t \geq m\right)\leq \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \geq m\right)<1-\delta\]
This contradicts the fact that $A^*_t$ is a feasible (and optimal) solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. Therefore, for sufficiently large $m$:
\[m^*(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1} A_t^* \geq c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)\]
Combining both bounds gives us:
\[m^*(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1} A_t^* \geq c_0\left(m +\max\{-\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m},\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)\right)\]
This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: p=1: condition on a good concentration event and reduce to the deterministic problem; p<1: contradiction via Berry-Esseen with the residual error.

    &\geq c_0\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty\left(\sigma-Tm^k+\varepsilon\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \left(\sigma-Tm^k\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ o\left(\left(\sigma-Tm^k\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E}\right)\\
    &+ o(1)\\
    &\geq c_0\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty\sigma\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E}\right)+c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot\zeta_T\cdot\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty(\sigma-Tm^k)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t=\sigma\mid \mathcal{E}\right)\\
    &+ o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\quad\text{(because $k<\alpha_T(1-r)$)}\\
    &\geq c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)
    \quad\text{(Lemma~\ref{lem:sum_bound})}
\end{align*}
The proof is completed since $\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t\right]\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}\right] + o(1)$. 

\underline{Case 2: $p\neq 1$.}

First, we could follow the same logic as in the proof for $p=1$, and get:
\[m^*(\varepsilon,T) \geq c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\]

This bound is tight if $\alpha_T(1-r)\geq1/2$, since the upper-bounding solution admits a buffer of $\Theta(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)})$ in that case; however, if $\alpha_T(1-r)<1/2$, the bound may no longer be tight since the the upper-bounding buffer then grows in $\Theta(\sqrt{m})$. To improve it, we assume by contradiction that:
\[m^*(\varepsilon,T)=\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t <c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)\]
Consider independent trials $S'_{it} \sim \mathrm{Bern}\left(1-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$ and define $B'_t = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}_t} S'_{it}$. We have:
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t \geq m\right)\leq \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \geq m\right)\]
Then by the Berry-Esseen Theorem, we have:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t<m \right)
    =&\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t -\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \right] <m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p)) \right)
    \\=&\Phi\left(\frac{m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)}}\right) + \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\sum_{t=1}^TA^*_t(1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)(2\varepsilon(1-p)-1)}{\left(\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)\right)^{3/2}}\right)
    \\=&\Phi\left(\frac{m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)}}\right) + o(1)
\end{align*}
We use the contradiction assumption $\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t < c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)$ to bound the numerator and the fact that $\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t<2c_0m$ to bound the denominator. We obtain
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t<m \right)> &\Phi\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}}{\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}}\right) + o(1)   =\delta +o(1)
\end{align*}
Therefore, for sufficiently large $m$:
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t \geq m\right)\leq \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \geq m\right)<1-\delta\]
This contradicts the fact that $A^*_t$ is a feasible (and optimal) solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. Therefore, for sufficiently large $m$:
\[m^*(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1} A_t^* \geq c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)\]
Combining both bounds gives us:
\[m^*(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1} A_t^* \geq c_0\left(m +\max\{-\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m},\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)\right)\]
This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Define the good event E
nodes.statement:
Let $k$ be such that $\frac{1}{2}\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)<k<\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)$. Let us define the following ``good'' event:
$$\mathcal{E}=\left\{\left|B_t - A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\right|\leq m^k,\ \forall t \in \{1,\cdots, T\}\right\}$$
