nodes.name: Good-event probability (core model)
nodes.statement: If $A_t\leq m+ \mathcal{O}(m^{\alpha_T \cdot (1-r)})$ for all $t=1,\cdots, T$, then $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^c) =\mathcal{O}(\exp\left(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right))$ as $m \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Each B_t stays within m^k of its mean for all t, except with exponentially small probability.
nodes.label: lem:hoeffding_bound

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (good-event probability)
nodes.statement:
By construction, $\mathbb{E}[B_t] = A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\leq A_t$. From Bernstein's inequality, using the definition of $B_t=\sum_{i:y_{it}=1}S_{it}$:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{P}(|B_t - \mathbb{E}[B_t]| \geq m^k)
        &\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{1/2\cdot m^{2k}}{\sum_{i:y_{it}=1}\text{Var}(S_{it})+1/3\cdot m^k}\right)\\
        &= 2\exp\left(-\frac{1/2\cdot m^{2k}}{\text{Var}(B_t)+1/3\cdot m^k}\right)\\
        &\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{m^{2k}}{4\varepsilon \zeta_T m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + 2m^k/3}\right)\\
        &= \mathcal{O}\left(\exp\left(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right),
    \end{align*}
    where the equality follows from the independence of $B_1,\cdots,B_T$ and the second inequality uses the lower bound on the variance term from the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:main_feasible}. By assumption, $2k - \alpha_T\cdot(1-r) > 0$, so $\mathbb{P}\left(|B_t - \mathbb{E}[B_t]| \geq m^k\right) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. We obtain from the union bound:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^c)
    &=\mathbb{P}\left(\exists t \in \{1,\cdots, T\} \;\; : \;\; \left|B_t - A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\right|\geq m^k\right)\\
    &\leq \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{P}\left(\left|B_t - A_t \left(1 -\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}\right)\right|\geq m^k\right)\\
    & =\mathcal{O}(\exp\left(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right))
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding_bound}.
nodes.statement_short: Bernstein's inequality per period with the variance bound, then a union bound over periods.

We obtain from the union bound:

nodes.statement:
Similarly:
\begin{align*}
    &\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty(\sigma-Tm^k)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*
    =\sigma\mid \mathcal{E} \right)\\
    &\geq (m-Tm^k)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B_t^*\geq m\mid \mathcal{E} \right)\\
    &= m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}(1-Tm^{k-1})^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\left(1-o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)-1}\right)\right)\\

nodes.statement:
Now, let $(A^*_1,\cdots,A^*_T)$ and $(B^*_1,\cdots,B^*_T)$ denote the optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. We obtain from Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding_bound}:
\begin{align*}

    &\geq \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}\right]\left(1-\mathcal{O}(\exp(-m^{2k-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}))\right)\\
    &=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}\right] + o(1)
\end{align*}

\underline{Case 2: $p\neq 1$.}

First, we could follow the same logic as in the proof for $p=1$, and get:
\[m^*(\varepsilon,T) \geq c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\]

This bound is tight if $\alpha_T(1-r)\geq1/2$, since the upper-bounding solution admits a buffer of $\Theta(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)})$ in that case; however, if $\alpha_T(1-r)<1/2$, the bound may no longer be tight since the the upper-bounding buffer then grows in $\Theta(\sqrt{m})$. To improve it, we assume by contradiction that:
\[m^*(\varepsilon,T)=\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t <c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)\]
Consider independent trials $S'_{it} \sim \mathrm{Bern}\left(1-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$ and define $B'_t = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}_t} S'_{it}$. We have:
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t \geq m\right)\leq \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \geq m\right)\]
Then by the Berry-Esseen Theorem, we have:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t<m \right)
    =&\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t -\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \right] <m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p)) \right)
    \\=&\Phi\left(\frac{m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)}}\right) + \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\sum_{t=1}^TA^*_t(1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)(2\varepsilon(1-p)-1)}{\left(\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)\right)^{3/2}}\right)
    \\=&\Phi\left(\frac{m-\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t (1-\varepsilon(1-p))\varepsilon(1-p)}}\right) + o(1)
\end{align*}
We use the contradiction assumption $\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t < c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)$ to bound the numerator and the fact that $\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t<2c_0m$ to bound the denominator. We obtain
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t<m \right)> &\Phi\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}}{\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}}\right) + o(1)   =\delta +o(1)
\end{align*}
Therefore, for sufficiently large $m$:
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B^*_t \geq m\right)\leq \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t=1}^T B'_t \geq m\right)<1-\delta\]
This contradicts the fact that $A^*_t$ is a feasible (and optimal) solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. Therefore, for sufficiently large $m$:
\[m^*(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1} A_t^* \geq c_0\left(m -\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m}\right)\]
Combining both bounds gives us:
\[m^*(\varepsilon, T)=\sum_{t=1} A_t^* \geq c_0\left(m +\max\{-\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m},\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)\right)\]
This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Combine upper and lower bounds (Section 9.5)
nodes.statement:
The main result follows directly from the lemmas. Per Lemma~\ref{lem:main_feasible}, the solution given in Algorithm~\ref{ALG} is feasible in Problem~\eqref{prob:main}. Per Equations~\eqref{eq:solution} and~\eqref{eq:solution_eq}, it achieves an upper bound of:
$$m^\dagger(\varepsilon,T)=\begin{cases}
        c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  \sqrt{\frac{c_0}{2}\log \frac{2}{\delta}}\sqrt{m}\right) &  \text{if }p\neq 1\\
   c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right) &  \text{if }p=1
\end{cases}$$
 Moreover, per Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lower}, the optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main} admits a lower bound of
  \[m^*(\varepsilon, T) \geq   \begin{cases}
  c_0\left(m +\max\{-\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m},\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\}\right) +o\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)& \text{if }p \neq 1\\
      c_0\left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right) & \text{if }p=1
  \end{cases}\]
This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Upper bound from the allocation equations
nodes.statement:
Per Equations~\eqref{eq:solution} and~\eqref{eq:solution_eq}, it achieves an upper bound of:
$$m^\dagger(\varepsilon,T)=\begin{cases}
        c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  \sqrt{\frac{c_0}{2}\log \frac{2}{\delta}}\sqrt{m}\right) &  \text{if }p\neq 1\\
   c_0\left( m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot \zeta_T \cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right) &  \text{if }p=1
\end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound from the allocation equations

nodes.name: Lower bound from Lemma main_lower
nodes.statement:
Moreover, per Lemma~\ref{lem:main_lower}, the optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:main} admits a lower bound of
  \[m^*(\varepsilon, T) \geq   \begin{cases}
  c_0\left(m +\max\{-\Phi^{-1}(\delta)\sqrt{2\varepsilon(1-p)m},\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\}\right) +o\left(m^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)& \text{if }p \neq 1\\
      c_0\left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} +  o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right) & \text{if }p=1
  \end{cases}\]
This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound from Lemma main_lower

nodes.name: Problem with offline data Q*_T(m,N_0)
nodes.statement:
We define Problem~\eqref{prob:QtmN} as follows, with $N_0=\gamma m^\beta+\mathcal{O}\left(m^\beta\right)$:
\begin{align}
    \min\quad & \sum_{t=1}^{T}A_t \tag{$\mathcal{Q}^*_T(m,N_0)$}\\
    \text{s.t.}\quad&\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^TB_t\geq m\right] \geq 1-\delta \nonumber\\
    \quad& B_t\sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A_t, 1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_0\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right),\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber\\
    \quad& A_t,B_t\geq0,\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber
\end{align}

nodes.statement: Let $m^D(\varepsilon, T)$ be the optimal objective value of Problem~\eqref{prob:QtmN}, and $A^{D}_1,\cdots, A^{D}_T$ be its solution. For any $T\geq 2$, we have as $m \to \infty$: \begin{align*} & A^{D}_t = r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot \left(\frac{c_0}{\gamma}\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot m^{(1-\beta)\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right) + \beta}+o\left(m^{(1-\beta)\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right) + \beta}\right),\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T\\ &m^D(\varepsilon, T) = c_0 \left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma^{-\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)}\right)+o\left(m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)}\right). \end{align*}

nodes.name: New boundary conditions g(0)=gamma, f(0)=beta
nodes.statement:
The difference comes from the boundary condition. 
Let us write $u_t = \Theta(g(t)m^{f(t)})$ toward our leading-order and leading-coefficient analyses. Since $u_0 = \gamma m^\beta + o(m^\beta)$, we now have $g(0)=\gamma$ and $f(0)=\beta$. Moreover, since the solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:QtmN_det} is upper bounded by that to Problem~\eqref{prob:main_det}, we still have $g(T)=c_0$ and $f(T)=1$.

nodes.name: Leading-order exponents
nodes.statement:
We perform the same leading-order analysis as in Lemma~\ref{lem:main_det}, with $f(T)-f(0)=1-\beta$ instead of $f(T)-f(0)=1$. Therefore:
\begin{align*}
	& f(T)-f(0)=1-\beta=\frac{K}{1-r}\left(1-r^T\right)\\
	& f(t+1)-f(t)=Kr^t=(1-\beta)\cdot r^{t}\cdot\frac{1-r}{1-r^T}\\
	& f(t)=\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}(f(s+1)-f(s))+\beta=(1-\beta)\cdot\frac{1-r}{1-r^T}\cdot\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}r^s+\beta=(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T(1-r^t)+\beta
\end{align*}

In conclusion, the leading-order analysis leads to:
$$u_t=\Theta\left(m^{(1-\beta)\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right) + \beta}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Leading-order exponents

nodes.name: Sum the learning losses
nodes.statement:
We conclude as follows:
\begin{align*}
   &\left(1-(1-p)\varepsilon)\right)\sum_{t=1}^T A^D_t\\
   &= m + \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{A^D_t \cdot\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^D_s +1\right)^r}\\
   &=  m + \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p(u_t-u_{t-1})}{u^r_{t-1}}\\
   &= m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot  \sum_{t=1}^T r^{-\frac{\overline{h}(t)-r\overline{h}(t-1)}{1-r}}\cdot \left(\frac{c_0}{\gamma}\right)^{f(t)-rf(t-1)}\cdot m^{\overline{f}(t)-r\overline{f}(t-1)}+o\left(m^{\overline{f}(t)-r\overline{f}(t-1)}\right)\\
   &= m +\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\left(\sum_{t=1}^T \frac{1}{r^t}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^{\frac{r}{1-r}}\cdot r^{T\cdot\alpha_T}\cdot \left(\frac{c_0}{\gamma}\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\cdot m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)}+ o\left(m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)}\right)\\
   &= m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma^{-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\cdot m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)}+ o\left(m^{(1-\beta)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta(1-r)}\right)
\end{align*}
This concludes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:QtmN_det}.

nodes.name: Deterministic solution with offline data acquisition
nodes.statement: Let $m^D(\varepsilon, T)$ be the optimal objective value of Problem~\eqref{prob:ws_det}, and $A^{D}_1,\cdots, A^{D}_T$ be its solution. Define $\gamma_\star=\left(\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)c_0\varepsilon\cdot p \zeta_T}{c}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}$. For any $T\geq 2$, we have as $m \to \infty$: \begin{align*} & A^{D}_t = r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot \left(\frac{c_0}{\gamma_\star}\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot m^{\alpha_{T+1}(1-r^{t+1})}+ o\left(m^{\alpha_{T+1}(1-r^{t+1})}\right),\ \forall t=1,\cdots,T\\ &m^D(\varepsilon, T) = c_0m+\left(c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma_\star^{-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+c\cdot\gamma_\star\right)m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}+ o\left(m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}\right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Optimal acquisition A_0 = gamma_star m^{(1-r)alpha_{T+1}}; the regret term becomes order m^{(1-r)alpha_{T+1}}.
nodes.label: lem:ws_det

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (deterministic solution with acquisition)
nodes.statement:
Let us define $\gamma_\star>0$ and $\beta_\star\in[0,1)$ such that $A_0^D=\gamma_\star\cdot m^{\beta_\star}+o\left(m^{\beta_\star}\right)$. Unlike in Lemma~\ref{lem:QtmN_det}, $\gamma_\star$ and $\beta_\star$ are decision variables, reflecting the amount of offline data to be acquired. As in Lemma~\ref{lem:QtmN_det}, we can define $u_t = A^D_0 + \sum_{s=1}^t A^{D}_s + 1$ for $t=1,\cdots,T$, and derive:
\begin{equation*}
    u_t=r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot \left(\frac{c_0}{\gamma_\star}\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot m^{(1-\beta_\star)\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right) + \beta_\star}+o\left(m^{(1-\beta_\star)\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right) + \beta_\star}\right),
\end{equation*}
which achieves an objective of
$$c_0 \left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma_\star^{-\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot m^{(1-\beta_\star)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta_\star(1-r)}\right)+o\left(m^{(1-\beta_\star)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta_\star(1-r)}\right).$$

By construction, $A^D_0 = \gamma_\star\cdot m^{\beta_\star}+ o(m^{\beta_\star})$ and therefore the full objective value is:
\[ c_0m + \Theta\left(m^{(1-\beta_\star)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta_\star(1-r)}\right) + \Theta\left(m^{\beta_\star}\right)\]
As $m \to \infty$, the minimum is achieved when:
$$(1-\beta_\star)\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)+\beta_\star(1-r)=\beta_\star$$
Solving this equation gives $\beta_\star=\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)}{r+\alpha_T(1-r)}$. Recalling the definition of $\alpha_T=\frac{1}{1-r^T}$, we obtain: $\beta_\star=\frac{1-r}{1-r^{T+1}}=(1-r)\alpha_{T+1}$. We get $A^D_0 = \gamma_\star\cdot m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}$ and:
\begin{equation*}
    u_t=r^{-\frac{1}{1-r}\left(t-T\cdot\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)\right)}\cdot \left(\frac{c_0}{\gamma_\star}\right)^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r^t)}\cdot m^{\alpha_{T+1}(1-r^{t+1})}+o\left(m^{\alpha_{T+1}(1-r^{t+1})}\right)
\end{equation*}

Proceeding as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:QtmN_det}, we derive:
\begin{align*}
   \left(1-(1-p)\varepsilon)\right)\sum_{t=1}^T A^D_t
   &= m+\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma_\star^{-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\cdot m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}+ o\left(m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}\right)
\end{align*}

The optimal objective value is therefore:
$$c_0m+\left(c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma_\star^{-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+c\cdot\gamma_\star\right)m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}+ o\left(m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}\right)$$

Minimizing over $\gamma_\star$ yields the desired expression:
$$\gamma_\star=\left(\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)c_0\varepsilon\cdot p \zeta_T}{c}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}$$
Then, we have:
\begin{align*}
	c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma_\star^{-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+c\cdot\gamma_\star
	&= c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \left(\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)c_0\varepsilon\cdot p \zeta_T}{c}\right)^{-\frac{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}+c\left(\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)c_0\varepsilon\cdot p \zeta_T}{c}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}\\
	&= \left(c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot c^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot\alpha_T(1-r)\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}\cdot \left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)
\end{align*}
Therefore, the optimal objective value can be written as:
$$c_0m+\left(c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot c^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot\alpha_T(1-r)\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}\cdot \left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}+ o\left(m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}\right)$$
This concludes the proof of Lemma~\ref{prob:ws_det}, hence of the theorem.

$$\gamma_\star=\left(\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)c_0\varepsilon\cdot p \zeta_T}{c}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}$$
Then, we have:
\begin{align*}
	c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \gamma_\star^{-\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+c\cdot\gamma_\star
	&= c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot \left(\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)c_0\varepsilon\cdot p \zeta_T}{c}\right)^{-\frac{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}+c\left(\frac{\alpha_T(1-r)c_0\varepsilon\cdot p \zeta_T}{c}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}\\
	&= \left(c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot c^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot\alpha_T(1-r)\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}\cdot \left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)
\end{align*}
Therefore, the optimal objective value can be written as:
$$c_0m+\left(c_0\cdot\varepsilon\cdot p\cdot\zeta_T\cdot c^{\alpha_T(1-r)}\cdot\alpha_T(1-r)\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)+1}}\cdot \left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha_T(1-r)}\right)m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}+ o\left(m^{(1-r)\cdot\alpha_{T+1}}\right)$$
This concludes the proof of Lemma~\ref{prob:ws_det}, hence of the theorem.

nodes.name: Algorithm 5: adaptive re-optimization
nodes.statement: \caption{Adaptive algorithm to solve Problem $(\mathcal{P}^*)$.}\small \begin{algorithmic} \item Repeat, for $t=1,\cdots,T-1$: \begin{itemize} \item[] \textbf{1. Optimize.} Define $\beta_t=\alpha_T\left(1-r^{t-1}\right)$ and $\gamma_t$ such that $\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s=\gamma_t m^{\beta_t}+o\left(m^{\beta_t}\right)$. Solve Problem $\left(\mathcal{Q}^*_{T-t+1}\left(m-\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}B^{\textsc{ad}}_s,\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s\right)\right)$. Retrieve solution $A^\dagger_1,\cdots,A^\dagger_{T-t+1}$. \item[] \textbf{2. Commit immediate decision.} Implement the first-period decision: $A^{\textsc{ad}}_t=A^\dagger_1$. \item[] \textbf{3. Observe realizations.} Sample $B^{\textsc{ad}}_t\sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A^{\textsc{ad}}_t, 1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$. \end{itemize} \item $A^{\textsc{ad}}_T\gets\left(\mathcal{S}^*\left(m-\sum_{s=1}^{T-1}B^{\textsc{ad}}_s,\sum_{s=1}^{T-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s\right)\right)$. Sample $B^{\textsc{ad}}_T\sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A^{\textsc{ad}}_T, 1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{T-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$. \end{algorithmic}
also_stated_at: Upon solving Problem~\eqref{prob:main}, this approach derives the solution $A^\dagger_1,\cdots,A^\dagger_T$, but merely implements the first-period decision $A^\dagger_1$. Upon observing the realization $B_1$, the decision-maker solves a corresponding variant to open $m-B_1$ facilities over the remaining $T-1$ periods; it implements the second-period decision $A^\dagger_2$, and the procedure proceeds iteratively.
nodes.statement_short: Each period re-solve the remaining problem with offline data, implement only its first decision; final period solves S* exactly.
nodes.label: alg:adaptive

Solve Problem $\left(\mathcal{Q}^*_{T-t+1}\left(m-\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}B^{\textsc{ad}}_s,\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s\right)\right)$. Retrieve solution $A^\dagger_1,\cdots,A^\dagger_{T-t+1}$.

Sample $B^{\textsc{ad}}_T\sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A^{\textsc{ad}}_T, 1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{T-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$.

nodes.name: Claim to prove by induction over t
nodes.statement: Problem~$\left(\mathcal{Q}^*_{T-t+1}\left(m-\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}B_s,\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s\right)\right)$ is solved via Equations $\mathcal{A}(T,m,\gamma,\beta)$ and $\mathcal{L}(T,m,\gamma,\beta)$ using $\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s=\Theta(\gamma m^\beta)$. We prove by induction over $t=1,\cdots,T-1$ that $$A^{\textsc{ad}}_t=\Theta\left(m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^t\right)}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Claim to prove by induction over t

nodes.name: Base case from Theorem main
nodes.statement: The result for $t=1$ follows directly from Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
nodes.statement_short: Base case from Theorem main

nodes.name: Inductive step via Lemma QtmN_det and exponent algebra
nodes.statement:
Let us assume that it holds for $t-1\in\{1,\cdots,T-2\}$ and prove it for $t$. In period $t$, the decision-maker solves $\left(\mathcal{Q}^*_{T-t+1}\left(m-\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}B^{\textsc{ad}}_s,\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s\right)\right)$, where $\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A^{\textsc{ad}}_s=\Theta\left(m^{\alpha_T\left(1-r^{t-1}\right)}\right)$ per the induction hypothesis. Let us denote by $\beta_t=\alpha_T\left(1-r^{t-1}\right)$. Let us momentarily assume that  $\delta=o\left(m^{(1-\beta_t)\cdot\alpha_{T-t+1}\cdot(1-r)+\beta_t(1-r)-1}\right)$. Then, per Lemma~\ref{lem:QtmN_det}, we know that the solution of that problem, denoted by $A^\dagger_\tau$, satisfies 
$A^\dagger_\tau=\theta\left(m^{(1-\beta_t)\alpha_{T-t+1}\left(1-r^\tau\right)+\beta_t}\right)$ for $\tau=1,\cdots,T-t+1$. By construction, the adaptive policy follows the first-period solution in the problem solved at time $t$, so that $A^{\textsc{ad}}_t=A^\dagger_1$. Therefore: $A^{\textsc{ad}}_t=\Theta\left(m^{(1-\beta_t)\alpha_{T-t+1}(1-r)+\beta_t}\right)$. We conclude the induction as follows:
\begin{align*}
    (1-\beta_t)\alpha_{T-t+1}(1-r)+\beta_t
    &=\left(1-\alpha_T(1-r^{t-1})\right)\cdot\frac{1}{1-r^{T-t+1}}(1-r)+\alpha_T(1-r^{t-1})\\
    &=\frac{1}{1-r^T}\left(\frac{(r^{t-1}-r^T)(1-r)}{1-r^{T-t+1}}+1-r^{t-1}\right)\\
    &=\frac{1}{1-r^T}\left(r^{t-1}(1-r)+1-r^{t-1}\right)\\
    &=\alpha_T(1-r^t)
\end{align*}

nodes.statement: \caption{Semi-adaptive algorithm to solve Problem $(\mathcal{P}^*)$.}\small \begin{algorithmic} \item Repeat, for $t=1,\cdots,T-1$: \begin{itemize} \item[] \textbf{1. Optimize.} Solve Problem $(\mathcal{P}^*)$ using Algorithm 1 from the paper. Retrieve solution $A^\dagger_1,\cdots,A^\dagger_{T}$. \item[] \textbf{2. Commit $T-1$ decisions.} Implement decisions $A^\dagger_1,\cdots,A^\dagger_{T-1}$. \item[] \textbf{3. Observe realizations.} Sample $B_t\sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A^\dagger_t, 1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1} A_s +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$, $t=1,\cdots,T-1$. \end{itemize} \item $A^\dagger_T\gets\left(\mathcal{S}^*\left(m-\sum_{s=1}^{T-1}B^\dagger_s,\sum_{s=1}^{T-1} A^\dagger_s\right)\right)$. Sample $B^\dagger_T\sim \mathrm{Bino}\left(A^\dagger_T, 1- \frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{T-1} A^\dagger_s +1\right)^r}-\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)$. \end{algorithmic}

Recall that the semi-adaptive procedure implements $A^\dagger_1,\cdots,A^\dagger_{T-1}$ from Algorithm~\ref{ALG}, and then solves Problem $\left(\mathcal{S}^*\left(m-\sum_{s=1}^{T-1}B\dagger_s,\sum_{s=1}^{T-1} A\dagger_s\right)\right)$ in period $T$. This is detailed in Algorithm~\ref{alg:adaptive_simple}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (networked): regular case and plan
nodes.statement:
Under the additional regularity assumption that the facilities of degree $d_\star$ can cover $\Omega(m)$ customers, the problem reduces to the case of Section \ref{sec:base}. Indeed, no matter how many facilities with degree $d_\star$ have been opened, there are always facilities with degree $d_\star$ for which \emph{none} of the connected customers have been tentatively covered to date (per Assumption~\ref{eq:regime}). Then, it is without loss of generality to restrict the problem to those facilities because they provide the largest incremental coverage. Therefore, the results from Section \ref{sec:base} directly apply in that case.

We will now focus on the case where the conditions does not hold. We will first prove the relationship between the solution of Algorithm~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} and the optimal solution of Problem~\eqref{prob:network} for any value of $p$ (Part 1 below). We then prove the relationship between the Problem~\eqref{prob:network} and the fully-learned benchmark when $p=1$ (Part 2).
\begin{itemize}
    \item[--]  Part 1: Algorithm~\ref{ALG_network} yields a feasible solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:network} such that
$$m^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)\leq m^*(\varepsilon, T)+\begin{cases}
	o\left(m^{\alpha_T \cdot (1-r)}\right)& \text{if }p=1 \text{ or } (p \neq 1 \text{ and } \alpha_T\cdot(1-r)>1/2)\\
	\mathcal{O}(m^{1/2}) & \text{if }p \neq 1\text{ and } \alpha_T\cdot(1-r)\leq 1/2        
\end{cases}$$
    \item[--] Part 2: regret of the optimal stochastic solution against the fully-learned solution when $p=1$:
    \[m^*(\varepsilon, T) = m^{\textsc{L}}(T)+\Theta\left(m^{g(r)}\right)\]
\end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: If degree-d_star facilities cover Omega(m) customers, reduce to the core model; otherwise prove Parts 1 and 2 separately.

nodes.name: Fully-learned network benchmark (P_N^L)
nodes.statement:
When $p=1$, the "fully-learned" information benchmark, referred to as Problem~\eqref{prob:network_perfect} is formulated as the following (deterministic) discrete optimization problem. Note that, under perfect learning ($p=1$) and full learning (benchmark problem), the success indicators $S_{it}$ are time-invariant and known, and denoted by $S_i$. Yet, unlike in the core setting, the benchmark does not admit a closed-form solution.
\begin{align}
    \min \quad & \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it} \tag{$\mathcal{P}_N^{\textsc{L}}$}\\
    \text{s.t.}\quad& \sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT} \geq  m \nonumber\\
    \quad&z_{it}=z_{i,t-1} + y_{it} \times S_i,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{F},\ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber\\
    & s_{jt} \geq z_{it} ,\ \forall j\in\mathcal{C},\ \forall i\in \mathcal{F}_j, \ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber\\
    \quad& z_{i0}=0,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{F}\nonumber\\
    \quad& y_{it}\in\{0,1\},\ z_{it}\in\{0,1\},\ \forall i\in \mathcal{F}, \ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber\\
    \quad& s_{jt}\in\{0,1\},\ \forall j\in \mathcal{C}, \ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber
\end{align}

Proof of Theorem (networked): reduction to graphs without central facilities
nodes.statement:
We assume that $\mathcal{F}^\textsc{ctl}(d_\star)=\emptyset$ without loss of generality. Consider the graph $\mathcal{G}'$ where all central nodes $\mathcal{F}^\textsc{ctl}(d_\star)\cup \mathcal{C}^\textsc{ctl}(d_\star)$ and all connecting edges are removed. Let the optimal values of the stochastic problem, our algorithm, and the fully-learned problem in $\mathcal{G}'$ as $m_0^*(\varepsilon, T)$, $m_0^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)$, and $m_0^{\textsc{L}}(T)$ respectively. We can construct solutions to the original problems (with $\mathcal{G}$) by adding all central facilities, so that
\begin{align*}
    & m^*(\varepsilon, T)\leq m_0^*(\varepsilon, T)\leq m^*(\varepsilon, T)+|\mathcal{F}^\textsc{ctl}(d_\star)|\\
    & m^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)\leq m_0^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)\leq m^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)+|\mathcal{F}^\textsc{ctl}(d_\star)|\\
    & m^{\textsc{L}}(\varepsilon, T)\leq m_0^{\textsc{L}}(\varepsilon, T)\leq m^{\textsc{L}}(\varepsilon, T)+|\mathcal{F}^\textsc{ctl}(d_\star)|
\end{align*}

Once we prove the theorem for any graph such that $\mathcal{F}^\textsc{ctl}(d_\star)=\emptyset$, we get $m_0^*(\varepsilon, T)=m_0^{\textsc{L}}(T)+\Theta\left(m^{g(r)}\right)$ and $m_0^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)=m_0^*(\varepsilon, T)+o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)$ or $m_0^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)=m_0^*(\varepsilon, T)+\Theta\left(m^{1/2}\right)$. Since the minimum order of terms is strictly larger than $k$, this implies per Assumption~\ref{ass:degree} that $m^*(\varepsilon, T)=m^{\textsc{L}}(T)+\Theta\left(m^{g(r)}\right)$ and $m^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)=m^*(\varepsilon, T)+o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)$ or $m^\dagger(\varepsilon, T)=m^*(\varepsilon, T)+\Theta\left(m^{1/2}\right)$.

We make use of several lemmas. The logic of the proof is summarized in Figure~\ref{fig:proof_network}. To prevent circular reasoning, we prove the lemmas in ascending order to derive a proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:network}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (order-m openings)
nodes.statement:
Let us prove the lower bounds and upper bounds separately.

\paragraph{Lower bounds.}

The lower bounds stem from the degree assumption: each facility covers up to $d_\star$ customers and $m$ customers need to be covered, so at least $m/d_\star$ facilities are required. Formally, $\pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y})=0$ if and only if $y_{it}=0$ for all $t=1,\cdots,T$ and for all $i\in\mathcal{F}_j$:
$$|\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)|\geq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)}\pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)=\sum_{j=1}^q \pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger) \geq m+\Delta_G(m)\geq m$$
Moreover:
\begin{align*}
    |\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)|
    &=\sum_{j=1}^q\boldsymbol{1}(\mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)\neq\emptyset)\\
    &\leq \sum_{j=1}^q\sum_{i=1}^n\boldsymbol{1}(i\in\mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger))\\
    &=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\boldsymbol{1}\left(i\in\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)\right)\times\sum_{j=1}^q\boldsymbol{1}(i\in\mathcal{F}_j)\right)\\
    &\leq d_\star|\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)|,
\end{align*}
due to the assumption that the degree is bounded by $d_\star$. We obtain that
$m\leq d_\star|\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y})|$.

Similarly, for the stochastic solution, we know that with probability $1-\delta$ the solution satisfies $\sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT} \geq m$. Conditioned on this event, we use the result above to write:
\[\mathbb{E}\left[|\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^*)| \mid \sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT} \geq m\right] \geq \frac{m}{d_\star}\]
We conclude:
\[\mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^*)|] \geq \frac{m(1-\delta)}{d_\star}\]

\paragraph{Upper bounds.}

Let us start with Problem~\eqref{prob:network}. Lemma~\ref{lem:main_feasible} provides an algorithm that tentatively opens $d_\star c_0\left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \Delta(m)\right)$ facilities over $T$ periods, so that at least $d_\star m$ facilities are actually opened with probability at least $1-\delta$. Per our degree assumption, each customer is connected to at most $d_\star$ facilities. Using the same argument as above, any set of $d_\star m$ facilities is connected to at least $m$ customers. This means that the solution satisfies the chance constraint, and defines a feasible solution to problem~\eqref{prob:network}. We have derived a solution that satisfies:
\begin{align*}
    &\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it} =d_\star c_0 \left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ \Delta(m)\right) \\
    & \mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n z_{it} \geq d_\star m\right] \geq 1-\delta\\
    & \mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT} \geq m\right] \geq 1-\delta
\end{align*}

Turning to Algorithm~\ref{ALG_network}, define $q=m+\Delta_G(m)$. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:main_bound}, there exists an algorithm such that tentatively opening the following number of facilities
$$\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^T y_{it}=d_\star c_0 \left(q + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot\zeta_T\cdot q^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \Delta(q)\right)$$
would result in the number of opened facilities in expectation such that:
\[\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^T z_{it}\right]  \geq d_\star q,\]
for $m$ sufficiently large. Again, since each customer is connected to at most $d_\star$ facilities, any set of $d_\star q$ facilities is connected to at least $q$ customers. Thus, the expected number of connected customers must satisfy:
\[\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT} \geq m\right]\geq\frac{1}{d_\star}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{t=1}^T z_{it}\right]\geq q\]\

Therefore, opening $d_\star c_0 \left(q + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot\zeta_T\cdot q^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \Delta(q) \right)$ defines a feasible solution for Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG}, hence an upper bound to $|\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)|$. Note that the function within the brackets is concave in $q$ and its derivative is less than 3 for $q$ sufficiently large. Therefore, we obtain:
\begin{align*}
    |\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)|&\leq d_\star c_0 \left(q + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot \zeta_T\cdot q^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \Delta(q)\right)\\
    &\leq d_\star c_0 \left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)} + \Delta(m)+3(q-m)\right)\\
    &= d_\star c_0 \left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ \Delta(m)+3\Delta_G(m)\right)
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:sol_bound}.

    &= d_\star c_0 \left(m + \varepsilon\cdot p \cdot\zeta_T\cdot m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}+ \Delta(m)+3\Delta_G(m)\right)
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:sol_bound}.

nodes.name: Chromatic number
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{A})$ define an undirected graph. A coloring of $\mathcal{G}$ labels each vertex by one color each such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color. The chromatic number $\chi(\mathcal{G})$ is defined as the smallest number of colors defining a coloring of $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.label: def:chromatic

nodes.name: Fractional chromatic number
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{A})$ define an undirected graph. A $b$-fold coloring of $\mathcal{G}$ labels each vertex with up to $b$ colors, such that no two adjacent vertices have any color in common. Its $b$-fold chromatic number $\chi_b(\mathcal{G})$ is defined as the smallest number of colors defining a $b$-fold coloring of $\mathcal{G}$. The fractional chromatic number, denoted by $\chi^*(\mathcal{G})$, is given by: $\chi^*(\mathcal{G})=\lim\limits_{b\to\infty}\frac{\chi_b(\mathcal{G})}{b}$
nodes.statement_short: b-fold colorings give chi_b; the fractional chromatic number is lim chi_b/b.
nodes.label: def:Fchromatic

nodes.name: Berry-Esseen bound for dependency graphs
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,\cdots, X_n$ be random variables in $[0,c_i]$. Let $\mathcal{G}$ denote the dependency graph of $X_1,\cdots, X_n$ and $\chi^*(\mathcal{D})$ denote its fractional chromatic number. Then we have: \begin{equation*} \mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^n X_i - \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right]\right|\geq s \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)}\right)=2\Phi(-s) +\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\max_{i} c_i \cdot \chi^*(\mathcal{G})^2 \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\left[(X_i-\mathbb{E}[X_i])^3\right]}{\left(\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)\right)^{3/2}}\right) \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Normal approximation for sums of bounded dependent variables, with error controlled by the squared fractional chromatic number of the dependency graph.

Each node represents a customer. An edge connects two customers $j$ and $k$ if and only if $s_{jT}$ and $s_{kT}$ are not independent, i.e., if and only if a facility that can cover both has been tentatively opened: $(j,k)\in\mathcal{A}\iff\mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{F}_k\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y})\neq\emptyset$

nodes.name: Brooks' theorem bounds the fractional chromatic number by d_
nodes.statement:
By assumption, the degree of any node in the customer-facility graph is less than or equal to $d_\star$. Therefore, any customer can share an adjacent facility with up to $d_\star(d_\star-1)$ other customers.
By Brooks' Theorem \citep{brooks1941colouring}, the chromatic number of $\mathcal{D}$ satisfies $\chi(\mathcal{D})\leq (d_\star)^2-d_\star+1\leq (d_\star)^2$. This implies that its fractional chromatic number satisfies $\chi^*(\mathcal{D})\leq \chi(\mathcal{D})\leq (d_\star)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Brooks' theorem bounds the fractional chromatic number by d_star^2

nodes.name: Variance of total coverage within chi* of the sum of varianc

We use this result to characterize $\left|\sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT} - \pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)\right|$. By definition, each variable $s_{jT}$ is bounded by 1. We also need to bound $\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{j=1}^q s^\dagger_{jT}\right)$. By definition of $\chi^*(\mathcal{D})$, $s^\dagger_{jT}$ is correlated to at most $\chi^*(\mathcal{D})$ other variables $s^\dagger_{iT}$. Using the inequality $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i)\leq n \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(X_i)$, we obtain
\[\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{j=1}^q s^\dagger_{jT}\right) \leq  \chi^*(\mathcal{D})\ \sum_{j=1}^q \mathrm{Var}(s^\dagger_{jT})\]

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (sensitivity to the target)
nodes.statement:
Lemma~\ref{lem:main_bound} provides an algorithm that tentatively opens $d_\star c_0 \left(\Delta+\mathcal{O}\left(\Delta^{g(r)}\right)\right)$ facilities and that opens at least $d_\star\Delta$ facilities on average, for sufficiently large $\Delta$. Again, due to our degree assumption, this implies that the solution will serve at least $\Delta$ customers.

Let us consider the solution $\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger(m-\Delta)$ and add $d_\star c_0\left(\Delta+\mathcal{O}\left(\Delta^{g(r)}\right)\right)$ more facilities that connect to customers separate from those that are served in the current solution $\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger(m-\Delta)$ (those exist per the assumption of Theorem \ref{thm:network}). This new solution serves $\Delta$ more customers than the solution $\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger(m-\Delta)$ in expectation. By proceeding as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:sol_bound}, we can prove that it is a feasible solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} with a coverage target of $m$. We get the following bound:
\[\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(m)\leq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(m-\Delta)+d_\star c_0 \left(\Delta+\mathcal{O}\left(\Delta^{g(r)}\right)\right)\]

Similarly, let us consider the solution $\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger(m)$ with a coverage target of $m$, and subtract $\frac{c_0 \Delta}{d_\star}$ facilities. By definition of $c_0$, every facility has at most $\frac{1}{c_0}$ chance of succeeding, and therefore, on average at most $\frac{\Delta}{d_\star}$ facilities can succeed. Per our degree assumption, each facility is connected to at most $d_\star$ customers, so $\frac{\Delta}{d_\star}$ facilities are connected to at most $\Delta$ customers. Therefore, the new solution covers at least equal as many customers as $\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger(m)$ minus $\Delta$ customers. The new solution is feasible for Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG} with a coverage target of $m-\Delta$. We obtain:
\[\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(m-\Delta)\leq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(m)-\frac{c_0 \Delta}{d_\star}\]
This completes the proof of the lemma.

By further conditioning on the value of $s^*_{jT}$ and defining $A^*_t = \sum_{i=1}^n y^*_{it}$, we obtain:
\begin{align*}
    m^*(\varepsilon, T)
    &\geq\sum_{\sigma=0}^\infty \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*), \sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}=\sigma\right]\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}=\sigma \mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*) \right) + o(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)})\\
    &\geq\sum_{\sigma=m}^\infty \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*), \sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}=\sigma\right]\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}=\sigma \mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*) \right) + o(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)})\\
    &\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*), \sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}=m\right]\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}\geq m \mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*) \right) + o(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)})\\
    &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T A^*_t \mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*), \sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}=m, \sum_{j=1}^q \pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^*)\geq m-\Delta_G(m)\right]\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j=1}^q s^*_{jT}\geq m\mid \mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^*) \right) + o(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)})
\end{align*}

nodes.name: Coverage probabilities of the fully-learned solution
nodes.statement: Consider an optimal solution $\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}}$ to Problem~\eqref{prob:network_perfect}. We have: \begin{align*} \sum_{j=1}^q\pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})&\geq m-\sum_{\tau=1}^T \sum_{i =1}^n \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}+\right)y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}\cdot d_\star\\ \sum_{j=1}^q\pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})&\leq m-\sum_{\tau=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau} \end{align*}

nodes.label: lem:bound_loss_gen

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (fully-learned coverage)
nodes.statement:
Under solution $y^{\textsc{L}}_{it}$, every facility is opened at most once throughout the planning horizon (since $p=1$ and we know the success indicators). This implies that: $\sum_{t=1}^Ty^{\textsc{L}}_{it}\leq 1, \;\;\forall i=1,\cdots,n$. Therefore, for the facilities $i\in\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})$, we can define the time $t(i)$ as the unique time period where facility $i$ was opened, i.e., $y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}=1$ and $y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,\tau}=0$ for all $\tau\neq t(i)$. By convention, $t(i)=0$ and $y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}=0$ if $i\notin\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})$. The lower bound is obtained as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{j=1}^q\pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})
     =&\sum_{j=1}^q \left[1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j=1}^q \left[1-\prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)^{y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j=1}^q \left[1-\prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \left[1-\prod_{i\in\mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     \geq& \sum_{j\in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \left[1-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \left[1-\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     =&|\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})|- \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_i\cap\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})}  \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}y\\
     \geq& m-\sum_{i =1}^n \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}\cdot d_\star}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\\
     =& m-\sum_{\tau=1}^T \sum_{i =1}^n \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}\cdot d_\star}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r},
\end{align*}
where the first inequality stems from the fact that $ab\leq a+b$ for any $a,b\in[0,1]$, and the second inequality stems from the feasibility of the solution $\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}}$ (which implies that $|\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})|\geq m$) and from the fact that $|\mathcal{C}_i|\leq d_\star$ per our degree assumption.

We denote by $\mathcal{M}_t(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})$ the set of customers first tentatively covered in period $t$:
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{M}_t(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})&=\left\{j\in\{1,\cdots,q\}:\exists i\in\mathcal{F}_j:y_{i1}=\cdots=y_{i,t-1}=0,\ y_{it}=1,\ y_{k\tau}=0,\ \forall \tau\leq t,\forall k\in\mathcal{F}_j\setminus\{i\}\right\}
\end{align*}
Since $\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}}$ is the optimal solution to the fully-learned problem, every opened facility must serve at least one customer that is not served by any other facility (otherwise, this facility can be removed, contradicting the optimality of the solution). Thus, if $y^{\textsc{L}}_{it(i)}=1$, we can denote such customer by $j^{\textsc{L}}(i)$. Then, we have:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{j=1}^q \pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})
    =&\sum_{j=1}^q\left[1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}}\right]\\
    =&\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}_t(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \left[1-\prod_{\tau=t}^T \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}}\right]\\
    \leq &\left(\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}_t(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} 1\right)-\left(\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}_t(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}}), \exists k\;s.t.\;j=j^{\textsc{L}}(k)}\prod_{\tau=t}^T \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}}\right]\\
    \overset{{(*)}}{=}& m-\left(\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}_t(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}}), \exists k\;s.t.\;j=j^{\textsc{L}}(k)} \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)y^{\textsc{L}}_{kt}\right)\\
    =&m-\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)\\
    =&m-\sum_{\tau=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}
\end{align*}

The starred equality comes from two observations. First, the coverage constraint is binding (i.e., $|\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})|=m$) due to the optimality of the fully-learned solution. Second, for $j\in \mathcal{M}_t(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})$ (i.e., customer $j$ is first tentatively covered at time $t$) such that there exists $k$ such that $j=j^{\textsc{L}}(k)$ (i.e., customer $j$ is only covered by facility $k$), the following holds: (i) $y^{\textsc{L}}_{kt}=1$; (ii) $y^{\textsc{L}}_{it} =0,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{F}_{j^{\textsc{L}}(k)}\setminus\{k\}$; and (iii) $y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau} =0,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{F}_{j^{\textsc{L}}(k)},\ \forall \tau\neq t$. This concludes the proof of the lemma.

\begin{align*}
    \sum_{j=1}^q\pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})
     =&\sum_{j=1}^q \left[1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j=1}^q \left[1-\prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right)^{y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j=1}^q \left[1-\prod_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \left[1-\prod_{i\in\mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     \geq& \sum_{j\in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \left[1-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}_j\cap\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \frac{\varepsilon}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     =&\sum_{j\in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})} \left[1-\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\right]\\
     =&|\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})|- \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_i\cap\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})}  \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}y\\
     \geq& m-\sum_{i =1}^n \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i,t(i)}\cdot d_\star}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t(i)-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r}\\
     =& m-\sum_{\tau=1}^T \sum_{i =1}^n \frac{\varepsilon\cdot y^{\textsc{L}}_{i\tau}\cdot d_\star}{\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\tau-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y^{\textsc{L}}_{is}+1\right)^r},
\end{align*}
where the first inequality stems from the fact that $ab\leq a+b$ for any $a,b\in[0,1]$, and the second inequality stems from the feasibility of the solution $\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}}$ (which implies that $|\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\textsc{L}})|\geq m$) and from the fact that $|\mathcal{C}_i|\leq d_\star$ per our degree assumption.

nodes.name: Sensitivity lemma gives the lower bound on m^L
nodes.statement:
Let us again denote $q=m+\Delta_G(m)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:gen_deter_sol_lower} implies:
\begin{align*}
   &\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger\left(m - d_\star K(T,\varepsilon,p)\cdot m^{g(r)}+o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)\right)\\
   &\geq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(m)-d_\star^2 K(T,\varepsilon,p) m^{g(r)} + o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)\\
   &\geq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(q)-d_\star \left((q-m)+\mathcal{O}\left((q-m)^{g(r)}\right)\right)-d_\star^2  K(T,\varepsilon,p) m^{g(r)} + o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)\\
   &=	 \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(q)-d_\star^2 K'(T,\varepsilon,p) m^{g(r)} + o\left(m^{g(r)}\right) 
\end{align*}
with
$$K'(T,\varepsilon,p)=\begin{cases}
	K(T,\varepsilon,p)& \text{if }p=1 \text{ or } (p \neq 1 \text{ and } \alpha_T\cdot(1-r)>1/2)\\
	K'(T,\varepsilon,p)+1 & \text{if }p \neq 1\text{ and } \alpha_T\cdot(1-r)\leq 1/2        
\end{cases} $$
Combining these observations, we obtain:
$$m^{\textsc{L}}(T)\geq\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(q)-\mathrm{d}_\star^2 K'(T,\varepsilon,p)\cdot m^{g(r)}+ o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)$$

nodes.name: Sensitivity lemma gives the upper bound on m^L
nodes.statement:
Again, using Lemma~\ref{lem:gen_deter_sol_lower}, we have:
\begin{align*}
   &\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger\left(m - K(T,\varepsilon,p)\cdot m^{g(r)}+o\left(m^{\alpha_T\cdot(1-r)}\right)\right)\\
   &\leq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(m)-\frac{1}{d_\star}K(T,\varepsilon,p)\cdot m^{g(r)} + o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)\\
   &\leq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(q)-\frac{1}{d_\star}\left((q-m)+\mathcal{O}\left((q-m)^{g(r)}\right)\right)-\frac{1}{d_\star}K(T,\varepsilon,p)\cdot m^{g(r)} + o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)\\
   &= \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(q)-\frac{1}{d_\star}K'(T,\varepsilon,p)\cdot m^{g(r)} + o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)
\end{align*}

Combining these observations, we obtain:
$$m^{\textsc{L}}(T)\leq\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^\dagger(q)-\frac{1}{d_\star}K'(T,\varepsilon,p)\cdot m^{g(r)} + o\left(m^{g(r)}\right)$$

nodes.name: Claim: Algorithm 2 is feasible for P_N*
nodes.statement:
We prove that Algorithm~\ref{ALG_network} yields a feasible solution to~\eqref{prob:network}. By definition of Problem~\eqref{prob:network_ALG}:
\[\sum_{j=1}^q \pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger) \geq m + \Delta_G(m)\]

Conditioned on $\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)$, we have:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{j=1}^q s^\dagger_{jT}&\geq \sum_{j=1}^q \pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)-\left|\sum_{j=1}^q (s^\dagger_{jT}-\pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)\right|\geq\sum_{j=1}^q \pi_{j}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger)-\Delta_G(m)\geq m
\end{align*}

This implies from Lemma \ref{lem:hoeffding_gen_bound} that $\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j=1}^q s^\dagger_{jT}\geq m\right)\geq \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}(\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger))\geq 1-\delta$. Therefore, the decision vector $\boldsymbol{y}^\dagger$ defines a feasible solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:network}.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary (no-learning baseline, network)
nodes.statement:
We define the no-learning problem as follows:
\begin{align}
    \min \quad & \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it} \tag{$\mathcal{P}_N^{NL}$}\\
    \text{s.t.}\quad&\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT} \geq m\right] \geq 1-\delta \nonumber\\
    \quad& s_{jT}\sim \mathrm{Ber}\left(1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \varepsilon^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y_{i\tau}}\right),\quad \forall j\in\mathcal{C}\ \nonumber\\
    \quad& y_{it}\in\{0,1\},\ \forall i\in \mathcal{F}, \ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}\nonumber
\end{align}

As in Lemma~\ref{lem:gen_deter_sol_lower}, let us define $\boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{NL}}(m-\Delta)$ as the solution to Problem~\eqref{prob:network_nolearn} with the constraint that $m-\Delta$ facilities must open with probability $1-\delta$:
\begin{align*}
    \boldsymbol{y}^{NL}(m-\Delta)\in\argmin \quad & \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it} \\
    \text{s.t.}\quad&\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT} \geq m-\Delta\right] \geq 1-\delta\\
    \quad& s_{jT}\sim \mathrm{Ber}\left(1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \varepsilon^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y_{i\tau}}\right),\quad \forall j\in\mathcal{C}\\
    \quad& y_{it}\in\{0,1\},\ \forall i\in \mathcal{F}, \ \forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\end{align*}

By the same argument as in Lemma~\ref{lem:gen_deter_sol_lower}, we have:
\[\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^{\mathrm{NL}}(m-\Delta) \leq\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n y_{it}^{NL}(m) - \frac{c_0\Delta}{d_\star} \]

Recall that $\sum_{t=1}^Ty^{\textsc{L}}_{it}\leq 1, \;\;\forall i=1,\cdots,n$ and that $|\mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{L}})|=m$. The expected customer coverage of the fully-learned solution in the no-learning problem satisfies:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^q s_{jT}\right]
    &= \sum_{j=1}^q\left(1-\prod_{\tau=1}^T \varepsilon^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y_{i\tau}^{\mathrm{L}}} \right)\\
    &=\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{L}})} \left(1 - \prod_{\tau=1}^T \varepsilon^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} y_{i\tau}^{\mathrm{L}}}\right) \\
    &=\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{L}})} \left(1 - \varepsilon^{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_j} \sum_{\tau=1}^Ty_{i\tau}^{\mathrm{L}}}\right) \\
    &\leq\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{L}})} \left(1 - \varepsilon^{d_\star}\right) \\
    &=  m - m \varepsilon^{d_\star}
\end{align*}

By the same argument as Lemma \ref{lem:network_deter_lower},
\[m^{\mathrm{L}}(T) \leq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{NL}}(m-m \varepsilon^{d_\star})\leq \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{NL}}(m) - \frac{c_0m \varepsilon^{d_\star}}{d_\star}=m^{\mathrm{NL}}(\varepsilon, T) - \frac{c_0m \varepsilon^{d_\star}}{d_\star}.\]
This proves that $m^{\mathrm{NL}}(\varepsilon, T)\geq m^{\mathrm{L}}(T)+\Omega(m)$.
nodes.statement_short: The fully-learned solution loses a constant fraction eps^{d_star} of coverage without learning; sensitivity of the target gives linear regret.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary (star graphs)
nodes.statement:
Consider two facilities $i_1\neq i_2$ such that $y^\dagger_{i_1,t}=y^\dagger_{i_2, \tau}=1$, with $t<\tau$. In the case of a star graph, we know that $\mathcal{C}_{i_1}\cap\mathcal{C}_{i_2}=\emptyset$ and that $|\mathcal{F}_j|=1$ for all $j\in\mathcal{C}$. Denote by $N_{t-1}$ the number of samples available at time $t=1,\cdots,T$. Then, the condition from Proposition~\ref{prop:small_first} reduces to:
$$\sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_1}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)\leq\sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_2}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right),$$
i.e.:
$$\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)\text{deg}(i_1)\leq\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)\text{deg}(i_1)$$
Since $t<\tau$, we know that $N_{t-1}\leq N_{\tau-1}$, which implies that $\text{deg}(i_1)\leq\text{deg}(i_2)$. This proves that facilities are tentatively opened by increasing degree order. We proceed similarly to show that those facilities that do not get selected have a smaller degree than those that do get selected.
nodes.statement_short: In a star graph Proposition small_first reduces to a degree comparison, so facilities open by increasing degree.

$$\sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_1}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)\leq\sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_{i_2}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right),$$
i.e.:
$$\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)\text{deg}(i_1)\leq\left(\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{\left(N_{t-1} +1\right)^r}+\varepsilon\cdot(1-p)\right)\text{deg}(i_1)$$

nodes.name: Earlier facilities have smaller degree
nodes.statement: Since $t<\tau$, we know that $N_{t-1}\leq N_{\tau-1}$, which implies that $\text{deg}(i_1)\leq\text{deg}(i_2)$. This proves that facilities are tentatively opened by increasing degree order. We proceed similarly to show that those facilities that do not get selected have a smaller degree than those that do get selected.
